paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.35:1 Rule 3.35 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.35. 1. Application of Rule … R. 329 should be read as applying to the time that the consent is endorsed on the proposed judgment or order. If the endorsement and delivery are by the law firm which is then the defendants' solicitor of record, the defendants' later dismissal of that firm, or its later withdrawal, does not nullify the consent. Octa Hage Enterprises Ltd. (314121 Alberta Ltd.) v. Bank of Credit & Commerce Canada (1988), 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 31 at 32 (C.A.). 2. Approval as to Form Is Not Consent The consent marked on the draft order was “Approved as to form”. It was signed by counsel on behalf of the defendant. I do not regard such a consent or approval as a consent to the substance of the judgment. It purported to be and was, in my opinion, nothing more than an agreement that the draft judgment incorporated the judgment that the trial judge had indicated he would pronounce and was in proper form. It would operate as well, in my opinion, to waive any procedural objection to the motion for the order. Baxter Travenol Laboratories of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Canada) Ltd. (1983), 45 N.R. 393 at 424 (Fed. C.A.). 3. Who Is Bound? Consent orders bind only the parties to them. The reality is that this consent order, like most consent orders, is a de facto settlement between the parties to it, which settlement is given judicial sanction. It is a matter of elementary law that A and B cannot agree to something which will adversely affect C's rights. C's agreement is also necessary. Oldham v. Vistula Mobile Home Park Ltd. (1988), 84 A.R. 32 at 48 (Master). 4. Consent Does Not Create Jurisdiction In Morawetz v. Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2024 ABKB 588, Justice Marion said: [58] A court cannot grant an order simply because parties present it with a consent order. The order must be something within the jurisdiction and power of the Court, because parties cannot confer jurisdiction to a court by agreement where no jurisdiction exists: Calgary (City) v Bagaric, 2022 ABKB 635 at para 12, citing Transalta Utilities Corporation v Young Estate, 1997 ABCA 349 at para 43; Sedgwick v Edmonton Real Estate Board Co-Operative Listing Bureau Limited (Realtors Association of Edmonton), 2022 ABCA 264; 1658586 Ontario Inc v Can-Am Lubricants Inc, 2014 ONSC 2673 at para 55. 5. Effect of Consent Judgments Although the judgment is a consent judgment, it has the same force and effect as a judgment after trial. Wensel v. Wensel, [1976] 2 W.W.R. 267 (Alta. T.D.), at 270, per Quigley J., affirmed, [1977] 1 W.W.R. 32 (Alta. C.A.). 6. Setting Aside Consent Judgment A consent judgment is not lightly to be set aside. To do so in our view would involve proof of it having been obtained by fraud or deceit. There is no element of that here. L. (D.P.) v. E. (P.A.) (1984), 60 A.R. 87 at 88 (C.A.). On the same topic, Madam Justice Kent said in Schettle v. Lavallee (1994), 153 A.R. 235 (Q.B.), at p. 236: Here, a consent judgment was signed and entered. I am bound by our Court of Appeal in Wensel, Re, [1977] 1 W.W.R. 32 … which held that once a consent judgment is signed by a Queen's Bench judge, as was done here, that judge or any judge with concurrent jurisdiction is functus officio. The only remedy that is available is an appeal of the judgment on the basis that the judgment was obtained by fraud or mistake. That would be for the Court of Appeal to decide. In Dizes v. Dizes (1999), 240 A.R. 14 (Q.B.), Deyell J. came to the same conclusion. An application was made to vacate a consent order (on the allegation that counsel had not been instructed to consent to the order). His Lordship, at p. 15, said: I am bound by our Court of Appeal decision in Wenzel v. Wenzel[sic], [1977] 1 W.W.R. 32 … which held that once a consent judgment is signed by a Queen's Bench judge, that judge or any other Queen's Bench judge is functus officio. The procedure that should have been followed by Timothy Dizes was to appeal the order of Justice Fruman. In Rozinsky v. Rozinsky, 2013 ABCA 113, 2013 CarswellAlta 370, 544 A.R. 334, 82 Alta. L.R. (5th) 344 the Applicant sought to set aside a consent desk divorce judgment on the basis that the Applicant had never instructed his then counsel to consent to it. At paragraphs 6–8, and 10-11, the Court said: [6] There is some authority for the proposition that a consent judgment, having the same force and effect as a judgment after trial, can only be set aside in exceptional circumstances such as fraud, deceit and mutual mistake. See for example the judgment of this Court in D.P.L. v. P.A.E. (1984), 60 A.R. 87. That case, however, did not consider the situation where counsel acted without authority. [7] We appreciate that a lawyer is presumed to have ostensible or apparent authority to settle a claim which he has been retained to commence or defend. Lawyers acting within the scope of their ostensible authority bind their clients even if they are acting without actual authority: Correia v. Danyluk, 2001 ABCA 148, 286 A.R. 117 at para. 11. [8] There is no suggestion on this record that the Respondent had any basis to conclude that the Appellant's then lawyer did not have actual authority to consent to the Ross Judgment. This appearance of actual authority, however, is not dispositive of this appeal. … [10] Even without the Respondent counsel's concession that the Macleod Order was interim in nature, we note that agreements pertaining to custody and access are not binding upon the Court. It is open to the Court in an appropriate case (for example, where counsel acted without actual authority in defiance of his client's instructions) to refuse to decide such issues finally and definitively in the context of a divorce judgment. See Stewart v. Stewart (1990), 112 A.R. 137 (C.A.). In the case at bar, Court approval is a condition precedent to resolving the corollary relief prayed for in the Ross Judgment. [11] Having concluded that the Appellant's instruction to former counsel to appeal the Macleod Order constitutes, in effect, directions not to agree to the Ross Judgment and its corollary relief, and mindful that the Court's intervention was necessary to carry out the agreement to proceed to a divorce judgment in circumstances where the Appellant's former counsel acted in defiance of express instructions, appellate relief is appropriate. 7. Interpreting a consent order In Cho v. Harmony Ceramic Dental Laboratory Ltd., 2024 ABKB 571, a dispute arose over the interpretation of an order which had been granted on consent. The question came back before Justice Jeffrey who had granted the consent order, but he noted, in paragraph 3, that “[a]ll judges are equally positioned to interpret a consent order's meaning and application.” Justice Jeffrey set out the approach to be taken in interpreting a consent order's meaning. His Lordship said: [4] A consent order results from the parties to it reaching their own agreement. The interpretation of a consent order, therefore, is not an inquiry into what the signing judge meant by the wording of the order. [5] The interpretation of a consent order follows the same approach as the interpretation of any other form of agreement between private parties. The Alberta Court of Appeal summarized that approach in Canadian Natural Resources Limited v Wood Group Mustang (Canada) Inc. (IMV Projects Inc.), 2018 ABCA 305, at para 97: The objective of contractual interpretation is to ascertain the intention of the contracting parties by reading the contract as a whole, giving the words used their ordinary and grammatical meaning, consistent with the surrounding circumstances known to the parties at the time of the formation of the contract. The words of any one provision must not be read in isolation but should be considered in harmony with the rest of the contract and in light of its purposes and … context: Ledcor Construction Ltd. v Northbridge Indemnity Insurance Co., 2016 SCC 37 at para. 27, [2016] 2 SCR 23; Tercon Contractors Ltd. v British Columbia (Transportation and Highways), 2010 SCC 4 at para. 64, [2010] 1 SCR 69. [6] I found additional guidance on the interpretation of agreements in the form of consent orders from the following authorities: Shell Canada Products v Sunterra Beef Ltd, 2016 ABCA 250; Larcencova v Makarenko, 2018 ABCA 417; and Custom Metal Installations Ltd v Winspia Windows (Canada) Inc, 2020 ABCA 333. The Consent Order here is what the Alberta Court of Appeal calls an “interlocutory procedural consent order”, not a “final consent order”: see Custom Metal Installations, at paras 42 to 59.

paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Judgment in default of defence and noting in default

paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to subrule (2) and Part 11, Division 8, if a defendant does not file a statement of defence or demand for notice, or if the defendant's statement of defence is struck out, the plaintiff may, on filing an affidavit of service of the statement of claim, (a) enter judgment against the defendant under rule 3.38 or 3.39, or (b) require the court clerk to enter in the court file of the action, in Form 14, a note to the effect that the defendant has not filed a statement of defence or demand for notice and consequently is noted in default. (2) A judgment in default of filing a statement of defence must not, without the Court's permission, be entered against a person who is represented by a litigation representative. (3) If the defendant has filed but has not served a statement of defence or demand for notice, the plaintiff may apply to the Court for a costs award against the defendant for anything arising from the defendant's failure. Alta. Reg. 128/2015, s. 3; 36/2020, s. 3

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.36:1 Rule 3.36 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.36. 1. Effect of Noting in Default Noting in default is tantamount to an admission. The effect of [noting in default] is … to deem the allegations made to be proven. Klinck v. Drinnan (1985), 41 Alta. L.R. (2d) 299 (Q.B.), at 306, per Lutz J. Binder J. in Dykes v. Goczan (1996), 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 425 (Q.B.), noted one exception to the general rule that a defendant noted in default is deemed to have admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim. At pp. 426-27, his Lordship said: The effect of the Sulef decision [Sulef v. Parkin (1966), 57 W.W.R. 236 (Alta. C.A.)] which was approved by the Supreme Court of Canada in McElroy v. Cowper-Smith (1967), 60 W.W.R. 85, and applied by Lutz, J. in the Klinck case, is that when a defendant is noted in default the legal position in Alberta is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim by the failure to deny them. There is, however, an exception, which is the basis of the [Spiller v. Brown, [1973] 6 W.W.R. 663 (Alta. C.A.)] decision, that where the court is not satisfied that the plaintiff has a cause of action, the Court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter. In that case, for example, the trial judge had a suspicion that the plaintiff was manoeuvring to remove other defendants from the action to avoid the need to prove that the defendant who had not filed a defence was guilty of gross negligence. 2. Costs and Noting In Default In Capital One Bank v. Calhoun, 2007 ABQB 151, 2007 CarswellAlta 306, 427 A.R. 322, 75 Alta. L.R. (4th) 218, plaintiffs in a number of actions that were included in the application had noted the defendants in default, and were now seeking judgments which awarded solicitor-client costs for steps taken before and after judgment. The plaintiffs submitted that the defendants were deemed to have admitted the existence of agreements, the terms of which provided that the defendants had agreed to pay solicitor-client costs. Lee J. held that costs, being within the discretion of the Court, had to be determined by the Court. At pp. 221-222, his Lordship said: 13 Counsel for the Applicants seems to be submitting that the effect of noting the Defendant(s) in default results in his clients' entitlement to solicitor-client costs because the Statement of Claim says that the credit agreement provides for solicitor-client costs. The noting in default has the effect of deeming the facts plead as true, but I do not see it this way. … 15 The Applicants herein are entitled to their liquidated claims, namely the principal and interest owing on their credit card debts because the defendants were noted in default. 16 However, there is a difference between the Plaintiffs' entitlement to a liquidated demand, and the Plaintiffs' entitlement to solicitor-client costs. The principle amount claimed is admitted as part of the noting in default process, however costs are always the discretion of the Court, even in the face of a specific agreement between the parties; and regardless of an agreement, costs are always taxable. 17 While it may appear to be a simple proposition that the agreements provide for solicitor-client costs, a quick review for example of the Masters' various decisions with respect to mortgage foreclosures and solicitor-client costs certainly reveal that there is often much to argue about it in terms of the wording of agreements, and claims for solicitor and client costs. 18 Even if the wording in the agreement, and the claim fit the appropriate wording, there is still discretion in the Court to determine costs, and within that discretion, there is still the amount of costs to be determined. … 21 I am also in agreement with the present apparent practice of the Clerk of the Court not to tax post judgment costs on a solicitor-client basis, unless a Judge orders a specific award of solicitor-client costs. It is the Court, and not the Taxing Officers of the Court, that grant Judgments. The parties require the Court's approval for post judgment solicitor-client costs.

paragraphs.text: 3.37. Application for judgment against defendant noted in default
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Application for judgment against defendant noted in default

paragraphs.text: (1) The plaintiff may, without notice to any other party, on proof of the plaintiff's claim, apply to the Court for judgment in respect of a claim for which default judgment has not been entered if (a) one or more defendants are noted in default, or (b) the defendant's statement of defence is struck out. (2) In the circumstances described in subrule (1) the plaintiff is entitled to a costs award. (3) The Court may do one or more of the following: (a) pronounce judgment; (b) make any necessary order; (c) direct a determination of damages; (d) adjourn the application and order additional evidence to be provided; (e) dismiss the claim or a part of it; (f) direct that the claim proceed to trial and that notice be served on every other defendant; (g) make a costs award in favour of the plaintiff.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.37:1 Rule 3.37 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.37. 1. Deemed Admission of Facts; Cause of Action Must Still Be Established In Toerper v. Hoard, 2011 ABQB 85, 2011 CarswellAlta 194, the defendant's Statement of Defence had been previously struck out. An application for judgment then came before Madam Justice Strekaf. Her Ladyship said that the defendant was deemed to have admitted the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim. At paragraphs 2–4, Strekaf, J. said: 2 Rule 3.37 of the new Rules of Court provides for an application to the court for judgment where a defendant has been noted in default or where the defendant's Statement of Defence is struck out. 3 The purpose of an assessment of damages is to determine the quantum of damages, rather than the liability for damages, provided that the facts deemed to have been admitted establish the cause of action. A defendant who is noted in default is deemed to have admitted the allegations of fact contained in the Statement of Claim. 4 This issue was addressed in the context of the predecessor provision to Rule 3.37 in the old Rules of Court in Robinson v. Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311, 450 A.R. 167, where Yamauchi J. stated at paragraphs 10–12: [10] The strongest statement on the effect of the Defendants' failure to file a statement of defence was made by the Supreme Court of Canada in McElroy v. Cowper-Smith, [1967] S.C.R. 425 at 428, where Spence J., considered the reasoning in Sulef v. Parkin (1966), 57 W.W.R. (N.S.) 236 (Alta. C.A.), and said: … in the province of Alberta upon default in defence the defendant is to be taken to have admitted the facts set out in the statement of claim. This is a decision of the highest court in Alberta on a point of practice in the province, and this court will not interfere under such circumstances. Therefore, the Defendant, as plaintiffs at trial, were not required to prove publication of the alleged libel. [11] Although Spence, J., was writing in dissent, many Alberta cases since that time have held that the effect of a noting in default is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by the failure to deny them, see e.g. Klinck v. Drinnan, [1985] A.J. No. 576; 66 A.R. 321 (Q.B.), Dykes v. Goczan, [1996] A.J. No. 432; 188 A.R. 352 (Q.B.) (“Dykes”); Syncrude Canada Ltd. v. Tibo Steel Products Ltd. et al., [2001] A. J. No. 736; 292 A.R. 368; 2001 ABQB 478; Dyck et al v. Wilkinson et al., [2004] A.R. Uned. 657; [2004] A.J. No. 1155; 2004 ABQB 731. More relevant to the case with which this Court is dealing is a statement by Harvey, C.J.A. in Brennan v. Arcadia Coal Co. (1929), 24 Alta. L.R. 236 (C.A.), at 448 (“Brennan”), where he said: The amount of damages to which the plaintiff was entitled could only be ascertained by an assessment but the evidence to be taken on such assessment would only be for the purpose of ascertaining the amount of, and in no sense the liability for, such damages which latter has been established by the facts alleged, and admitted by the Defendant by reason of its failure to deny them. [12] The mere noting in default, however, does not end the matter. In Dykes at para. 6, Binder J., based on Spiller v. Brown, [1973] 6 W.W.R. 663 (Alta. C.A.) (“Spiller”), said that there is an exception to the rule that the Defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by failure to deny them “where the Court is not satisfied that the Plaintiff has a cause of action, the Court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter.” This Court has reviewed the pleadings filed in this matter and has heard the testimony of Robinson and concludes that the Plaintiffs have a cause of action against the Defendants. In Boyer v. Boyer, 2024 ABKB 727, the defendant's pleadings were struck out as a contempt sanction. The question arose as to what extent the defendant could then participate in the subsequent trial. Justice Lema said: [52] Most of the no-defendant cases involve defendants noted in default, versus struck-pleadings defendants. [53] I find that the principles governing noting-in-default cases apply equally to those involving struck pleadings. [54] In both scenarios, the defendant has, or ends up with, no pleading in opposition to the statement of claim. [55] In the struck-pleadings scenario, the defendant ends up in the same position as if he, she or it had not defended in the first place. [56] Technically speaking, the plaintiff in a struck-pleadings scenario could note the defendant in default post-striking; however, that step appears unnecessary, with the striking accomplishing the same thing (no defence, or no more defence). [57] As I see it, the functional equivalence of the two scenarios is recognized in Rules 3.36 and 3.37, which provide the same consequences and next-step options for the Court and the parties i.e. whether no defence was filed or a defence was struck. … [62] The critical impact of a noting in default or pleading being struck is losing the ability to challenge the facts asserted in the opposing party's pleadings…. … [86] The admissions implied from a noting in default or defence striking do not extend to statement-of-claim positions on questions of law or questions of mixed fact and law. … [94] To this point, I have concluded that, because of the striking, Mr. Boyer is deemed to have admitted the factual allegations in Ms. Boyer's statement of claim. And that he cannot introduce evidence contradicting those allegations. [95] Can he introduce other (not-contradicting) evidence? Submit a brief? Make opening and closing statements? Cross-examine the plaintiff and her witness(es)? Take other steps? … [97] Rule 3.37(1) contemplates, at least in some circumstances, the plaintiff proceeding, and the court deciding, without notice to a struck or noted-in-default defendant. [98] I do not read that as necessarily translating to a bar on such a defendant participating e.g. where notice is given and the defendant wishes to participate. … [101] As noted earlier, no Alberta rule expressly bars a struck-pleadings defendant from participating in the trial of the matter i.e. where the plaintiff has notified the defendant of the trial and the defendant wishes to participate. … Justice Lema then reviewed several Alberta cases, and on the issue of whether a party whose pleadings have been struck can participate in the trial, said: [120] The cases featuring participation square better (i.e. than the no-participation cases) with the flexibility accorded by Rule 3.37(3), especially Rule 3.37(3)(b) (“make any necessary order”). [121] The “make any necessary order” power is sufficiently broad to authorize participation by a struck or noted-in-default defendant and to set its bounds. … [127] …I find that the Court has sufficient power under Rule 3.37(3)(b) (“make any necessary order”) to allow a struck or noted-in-default party to give evidence i.e. as long as it does not contradict any of the deemed-admitted facts in the plaintiff's claim, subject to considering the reason(s) for pleadings being struck (as here), as discussed further below. … [130] As I see it, Rule 3.37(3) – in particular, its “make any necessary order” element — allows the Court, in appropriate circumstances, to permit defined participation by a noted-in-default or struck-pleadings defendant. [131] Participation may be warranted where it promotes the fundamental purpose of the Rules i.e. “provid[ing] a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost-effective way” (Rule 1.2(1)). Particularly where the benefits of allowing participation, including “provid[ing] the court with a richer record on which to base its decision” and “allow[ing] for a fair [or fairer] adjudication of the issues” (per Mullin v Sherlock, 2018 ONCA 1063 (para 55)), outweigh the costs, including possible delays e.g. where a scheduled trial, built on one-party participation, might have to be pushed back to accommodate two-party steps. In TLA Food Services Ltd. v. 1144707 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 550, 2011 CarswellAlta 1540, 525 A.R. 1, 56 Alta. L.R. (5th) 363, Justice Shelley discussed the effect of noting a defendant in default. At paragraphs 18 and 24, Shelly, J. summarized the law: 18 Strekaf J., in Toerper v. Hoard, 2011 ABQB 85, discussed the effect of a defendant's failure to file a defence under R. 3.37, citing Robinson v. Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311, 450 AR 167 and McElroy v. Cowper-Smith, [1967] S.C.R. 425. These cases, and others cited therein, provide that under the old rules (Alta Reg 390/1968), in Alberta noting in default means that the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim are admitted by the defendant. (Robinson at para. 11; McElroy at p. 425 (per Hall J.) and 428 (per Spence J.). Strekaf J. applied these principles to the new Rule. I agree that these principles continue to apply. … 24 A summary of these principles follows: 1. When a defendant is noted in default, it is deemed to have admitted the allegations in the Statement of Claim; 2. Before granting default judgment the Court must still inquire as to whether a cause of action is made out in the Statement of Claim, and may direct a hearing on the matter; 3. A defendant who has been noted in default cannot adduce evidence to contradict the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim in the course of a hearing for the assessment of damages; 4. Quantum of damages may be assessed based on affidavit evidence; 5. R. 152 of the previous rules gives the Chambers judge discretion as to whether to grant default judgment ex parte based on affidavit evidence or to require that notice be given and an assessment set down for hearing. In Argent v. Gray, 2015 ABQB 292, a defendant had been noted in default. However, he would have had a defence under the Limitations Act. Justice Dario concluded that the defendant could not avail himself of that defence though the Plaintiff could still be required to prove its claim against the defendant: 44 Having been noted in default, Mr. McMillan cannot avail himself of the limitations defence applicable to the other Defendants. In Makowichuk v Makowichuk, 2013 ABCA 439, 60 CPC (7th) 448 at para 9, the Court of Appeal held: • The appellant's position is of course contrary to s 3 of the Limitations Act, the relevant portion of which provides: “the defendant on pleading this Act as a defence, is entitled to immunity from liability in respect of the claim.” In other words, it requires that the defence be pleaded in order to give rise to the immunity. The logical extension of the appellant's position is that the immunity is available without so pleading, indeed, without even filing the Statement of Defence. In our opinion, that position is without merit. 45 Nevertheless, given that Rule 3.37 allows a court to dismiss a plaintiff's claim notwithstanding a noting in default, I am satisfied that the Plaintiffs cannot succeed against Mr. McMillan unless they prove their claim against him …. 2. Service of Amended Statement of Claim when Defendant Noted in Fault In Clarke v. Deranger, 2006 ABQB 442, 2006 CarswellAlta 773, 400 A.R. 327, 64 Alta. L.R. (4th) 382, Macklin J. stated, at p. 334: 30 While Rule 144 of the Rules of Court does provide that a defendant “who fails to defend or demand notice is not entitled to notice of any subsequent proceedings in the action,” this can only refer to proceedings that relate to the allegations in the original statement of claim of which the defendant has either received, or been deemed to have received, notice. I am not prepared to interpret the Rule as having the effect of allowing a plaintiff to proceed against a defendant on new allegations of which the defendant has no knowledge when the defendant has been noted in default of filing a defence to the original statement of claim. 31 A defendant who is served, either personally or substitutionally, with a copy of a statement of claim, may decide not to defend the action because the allegations are true, they are insufficient to make out a case against the defendant, or for some other reason. However, the defendant's failure to file a defence to a statement of claim does not give the plaintiff carte blanche to amend the claim by adding serious allegations against the defendant which will expose him to liability, where he did not have any before, or increase his potential liability, and then to proceed as though the defendant has admitted those new allegations. 3. When the Court Doubts There Is a Cause of Action In Dykes v. Goczan (1996), 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 425 (Q.B.), the defendant had been noted in default but sought leave to tender evidence contradicting the facts set forth in the Statement of Claim. Binder J. dismissed the application, but agreed that leave could be granted if the Court were of the view that the plaintiff did not have a cause of action. At pp. 353-354, His Lordship said: …[W]hen a defendant is noted in default the legal position in Alberta is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim by the failure to deny them. There is, however, an exception, which is the basis of the Spiller[Spiller v. Brown, [1973] 6 W.W.R. 663 (Alta. C.A.)] decision, that where the court is not satisfied that the plaintiff has a cause of action, the court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter. In that case for example, the trial judge had a suspicion that the plaintiff was manoeuvring to remove other defendants from the action to avoid the need to prove that the defendant who had not filed a defence was guilty of gross negligence. 4. When Alternative Remedies Were Sought In TLA Food Services Ltd. v. 1144707 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 550, 2011 CarswellAlta 1540, 525 A.R. 1, 56 Alta. L.R. (5th) 363, a Plaintiff noted a Defendant in default. The Statement of Claim sought damages, rectification of the contract in dispute, and specific performance of the contract. Justice Shelley held that the Defendant was entitled to notice of which remedy the Plaintiff sought, and that an ex parte application for rectification was not appropriate. At paragraphs 53-54, her Ladyship said: 53 In Fenske v. Schneider, 2007 ABQB 164, Veit J. held that, where a plaintiff has sought alternative remedies, the defendant should be given notice of a motion by the plaintiff to seek one of those remedies. Veit J. noted “a default of defence is an admission of the facts pleaded, not of the conclusions of law or the assessment of damages” (at para. 11) and “that the appropriate remedy flowing from that breach is not a fact which [the defendant] can be taken to have admitted” (at para. 15). In Fenske the plaintiff sought either damages or specific performance in the Statement of Claim, and then sought specific performance in the application for default judgment. Veit J. refused the application, noting (at paras. 15-16): … not only does the Statement of Claim itself advances two possible remedies, the remedy of specific performance is a discretionary, equitable remedy which will only be granted after a review of all pertinent circumstances. Mr. Fenske may well have a strong claim for specific performance: Fossum, [1997] A.J. No. 1255, Holden, [2002] A.J. No. 1424, United Gulf Developments Ltd., [2004] N.S.J. No. 66, Spicer, [2005] A.J. No. 1074. That is not the point. The issue is that Ms. Schneider may well have a position concerning the request for specific performance as opposed to a request for damages; she is entitled to advance that position for the court's consideration. 54 Similarly here, TLA's Claim sought damages, rectification of the Contract, and specific performance. In my view, as in Fenske, notice must be given to the Defendants of TLA's choice of remedy so that they can advance a position in regards to the appropriate equitable remedy. I conclude that this is a further ground for denying TLA's application. 5. Effects of Noting in default or Striking of defence In Boyer v. Boyer, 2024 ABKB 727, Justice Lema discussed the possible effects of having a defence struck, or being noted in default: [52] Most of the no-defendant cases involve defendants noted in default, versus struck-pleadings defendants. [53] I find that the principles governing noting-in-default cases apply equally to those involving struck pleadings. [54] In both scenarios, the defendant has, or ends up with, no pleading in opposition to the statement of claim. [55] In the struck-pleadings scenario, the defendant ends up in the same position as if he, she or it had not defended in the first place. [56] Technically speaking, the plaintiff in a struck-pleadings scenario could note the defendant in default post-striking; however, that step appears unnecessary, with the striking accomplishing the same thing (no defence, or no more defence). [57] As I see it, the functional equivalence of the two scenarios is recognized in Rules 3.36 and 3.37, which provide the same consequences and next-step options for the Court and the parties i.e. whether no defence was filed or a defence was struck. … [62] The critical impact of a noting in default or pleading being struck is losing the ability to challenge the facts asserted in the opposing party's pleadings, as explained in the cases below, starting with Robinson v Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311 (Yamauchi J.): The strongest statement on the effect of the Defendants' failure to file a statement of defence was made by the Supreme Court of Canada in McElroy v. Cowper-Smith, 1967 CanLII 70 (SCC), [1967] S.C.R. 425 at 428, where Spence J. considered the reasoning in Sulef v. Parkin (1966), 1966 CanLII 638 (AB CA), 57 W.W.R. 236 (Alta. S.C.- App. Div.) and said: … in the province of Alberta upon default in defence the defendant is to be taken to have admitted the facts set out in the statement of claim. This is a decision of the highest court in Alberta on a point of practice in the province, and this court will not interfere under such circumstances. Therefore, the respondents, as plaintiffs at trial, were not required to prove publication of the alleged libel. Although Spence J. was writing in dissent, many Alberta cases since that time have held that the effect of a noting in default is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by the failure to deny them, see e.g. Klinck v. Drinnan, [1985] A.J. No. 576 (Q.B.), Dykes v. Goczan, [1996] A.J. No. 432 (Q.B.) (“Dykes”); Syncrude Canada Ltd. v. Tibo Steel Products Ltd., 2001 ABQB 478 (CanLII), [2001] A. J. No. 736 (Q.B.); Dyck v. Wilkinson, 2004 ABQB 731 (CanLII), [2004] A. J. No. 1155 (Q.B.). More relevant to the case with which this Court is dealing is a statement by Harvey C.J.A. in Brennan v. Arcadia Coal Co. (1929), 1929 CanLII 274 (AB CA), 24 Alta. L.R. 236 at 448 (C.A.) (“Brennan”), where he said: The amount of damages to which the plaintiff was entitled could only be ascertained by an assessment but the evidence to be taken on such assessment would only be for the purpose of ascertaining the amount of, and in no sense the liability for, such damages which latter has been established by the facts alleged and admitted by the defendant by reason of its failure to deny them. [paras 10-11] [emphasis added] [63] As Yamauchi J. discussed further, the court must be satisfied that the admitted facts add up to a cause of action and that it has jurisdiction to grant the requested relief: The mere noting in default, however, does not end the matter. In Dykes at para. 6, Binder J., based on Spiller v. Brown, 1973 ALTASCAD 76 (CanLII), [1973] 6 W.W.R. 663 (Alta. C.A.) (“Spiller”), said that there is an exception to the rule that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by failure to deny them “where the Court is not satisfied that the Plaintiff has a cause of action, the Court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter.” This Court has reviewed the pleadings filed in this matter and has heard the testimony of Robinson and concludes that the Plaintiffs have a cause of action against the Defendants. Plaintiffs' counsel argued that the pleadings, proof of service of the pleadings on the Defendants and the praecipe to note in default all provide this Court with jurisdiction to assess damages. This Court disagrees with that proposition based on the statement by Johnson J.A. in Spiller at para. 8, where he said, “Neither by pleadings nor admissions can a defendant give a court jurisdiction that it does not otherwise have,” see also Muscutt v. Courcelles (2002), 2002 CanLII 44957 (ON CA), 213 D.L.R. (4th) 577, 160 O.A.C. 1, 60 O.R. (3rd) 20, 13 C.C.L.T. (3rd) 161, 26 C.P.C. (5th) 206 at para. 50 (Ont. C.A.) (“Muscutt”). Thus, this Court must determine whether it has jurisdiction even in the face of the noting in default. [paras 12-13] [emphasis added] [64] As confirmed in Smith v Tuchscherer, 2024 ABCA 186: … when proceeding on default or after pleadings are struck, counsel and parties remain obliged to prove entitlement to the remedies sought and to respect the limits of the served pleadings: TLA Food Services Ltd v 1144707 Alberta Ltd, 2011 ABQB 550 [Shelley J.]. [65] Another dimension of participation is applying for relief under the Rules of Court. In the analogous context of a party being noted in default, the noted-in-default party is still a party for the purpose of “tak[ing] any other step under the Rules”, per Yaremchuk v Haight, 2001 ABCA 7 (considering the pre-2010 Rules): In my view, a party who is noted in default does not cease to be a party to the action and is entitled to utilize Rule 244.1 [dismissal-for-delay rule]. According to Rule 142(3) once a defendant has been noted in default he or she is no longer entitled to deliver a statement of defence or demand of notice. Furthermore, once the defendant has been noted in default: [a]ll the plaintiff has to prove, or the defendant is permitted to controvert, is the amount of the damages; for the cause of action itself, as stated in the plaintiff's claim, and the right to some damages in respect of it, is admitted by the defendant, by his suffering judgement to pass against him by default. T.W. Chitty, ed., Chitty's Archibold's Practice of the Queen's Bench Division, vol. 2, 14th ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1885) at 1336, as cited in Sulef v. Parkin and Breno (1966), 1966 CanLII 638 (AB CA), 57 W.W.R. 236 (Alta. C.A.) But I have not been provided with any authority or directed to any Rule which might otherwise limit the right of a defendant to take any other step under the Rules. [para 5] [emphasis added] [66] A noted-in-default party's participation rights (there too to apply to have the remaining party's action struck for delay) were again examined in Zivkovic v Zivkovic, 2009 ABQB 542 (Veit J.). [67] Zivkovic was decided under the former rules but with an awareness of the proposed new (circa 2010) rules, including Rules 3.36 and 3.37. [68] After considering Yaremchuk (cited above), Veit J. observed: The approach taken by our Court of Appeal is not the approach taken in other jurisdictions. For example, the Ontario Rules of Court specifically state that a defendant who is in default cannot ask for dismissal of an action for delay: see Rule 24.01. However, in Ontario, a defendant who is in default can apply to the court for leave to bring a motion other than a motion to set the default praecipe aside. While that approach may be more logically consistent, our Court of Appeal has effectively short-circuited the need to make an application to move under R. 244.1 [dismissal for long delay]. [para 31] [emphasis added] [69] She concluded: It appears to me that ALRI's proposed new Rules of Court [i.e. which became the 2010 Rules] do not clarify the issues raised by this motion [i.e. a noted-in-default party's rights]: proposed Rules 3.36(1)(b), R. 3.37(1)(a), [and] R. 4.33 do not appear to give more guidance that is present under the existing Rules. Given the increasing number of self-represented litigants, especially in family law matters, it might be useful to provide explicit direction to such litigants about, for example, the effect of not defending an action. [para 37] [emphasis added] [70] I echo Veit J.s comments, finding them equally applicable to a struck-pleadings scenario. In both scenarios, the 2010 Rules do not explicitly address the effect of a party being noted in default or having its pleadings struck. While Rules 3.36 and 3.37 (discussed further below) provide various options for the Court in such scenarios, they do not (or at least not expressly) address whether the defendant continues to have any right(s) to participate in the proceeding or, if so, the nature and extent of any such right(s). … [73] On another dimension of participation, a noted-in-default or struck-pleadings party continues to be entitled to copies of orders and judgments affecting them, per Rule 9.8: Unless these rules otherwise provide or the Court otherwise orders, the party who enters the judgment or order must serve a copy of the entered judgment or order on each of the other parties. [74] The core definition of “party” (Appendix to the Rules of Court) is “a party to an action.” Per Yaremchuk (cited above), a noted-in-default (or, by extension, struck-pleadings) litigant does not cease to be a party (para 5). [75] On the overall impacts of pleadings being struck, Shelley J. surveyed the Alberta noting-in-default case law (which I find applicable to the struck-pleadings scenario) in TLA Food Services Ltd v 1144707 Alberta Ltd, 2011 ABQB 550, distilling the following principles: 1. When a defendant is noted in default, it is deemed to have admitted the allegations in the Statement of Claim; 2. Before granting default judgment the Court must still inquire as to whether a cause of action is made out in the Statement of Claim, and may direct a hearing on the matter; 3. A defendant who has been noted in default cannot adduce evidence to contradict the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim in the course of a hearing for the assessment of damages; 4. Quantum of damages may be assessed based on affidavit evidence; 5. R. 152 of the previous rules gives the Chambers judge discretion as to whether to grant default judgment ex parte based on affidavit evidence or to require that notice be given and an assessment set down for hearing. [para 24] [emphasis added] [76] For reference, here is former R. 152: If a sole defendant has, or all the defendants have, been noted in default, the plaintiff may: a. apply ex parte to the court for judgment, and the judge hearing the application may i. upon proof of the plaintiff's claim by affidavit or otherwise, give final judgment or direct an accounting, [or] ii. set the matter over for a hearing on notice, and notice shall be given to a defendant in the same manner as hereinafter provided on assessment or b. set the matter down for assessment, giving at least 10 days notice of the date set for the assessment. [77] Justice Shelley's distillation has been found applicable in the new (2010) Rules era, as reflected by its endorsement in Smith (ABCA — cited above) and other decisions, including Lund v Quinn Maintenance Inc, 2020 ABQB 722 (Eamon J) (para 8); Simmer v Copithorne, 2018 ABQB 525 (Eamon J.) (para 6); Roberts v Safadi, 2018 ABQB 165 (Mandziuk J.) (para 8); and Argent v Gray, 2015 ABQB 292 (Dario J.) (para 45).

[98] I do not read that as necessarily translating to a bar on such a defendant participating e.g. where notice is given and the defendant wishes to participate. … [101] As noted earlier, no Alberta rule expressly bars a struck-pleadings defendant from participating in the trial of the matter i.e. where the plaintiff has notified the defendant of the trial and the defendant wishes to participate. … Justice Lema then reviewed several Alberta cases, and on the issue of whether a party whose pleadings have been struck can participate in the trial, said: [120] The cases featuring participation square better (i.e. than the no-participation cases) with the flexibility accorded by Rule 3.37(3), especially Rule 3.37(3)(b) (“make any necessary order”).

[121] The “make any necessary order” power is sufficiently broad to authorize participation by a struck or noted-in-default defendant and to set its bounds. … [127] …I find that the Court has sufficient power under Rule 3.37(3)(b) (“make any necessary order”) to allow a struck or noted-in-default party to give evidence i.e. as long as it does not contradict any of the deemed-admitted facts in the plaintiff's claim, subject to considering the reason(s) for pleadings being struck (as here), as discussed further below. … [130] As I see it, Rule 3.37(3) – in particular, its “make any necessary order” element — allows the Court, in appropriate circumstances, to permit defined participation by a noted-in-default or struck-pleadings defendant.

[131] Participation may be warranted where it promotes the fundamental purpose of the Rules i.e. “provid[ing] a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost-effective way” (Rule 1.2(1)).

Particularly where the benefits of allowing participation, including “provid[ing] the court with a richer record on which to base its decision” and “allow[ing] for a fair [or fairer] adjudication of the issues” (per Mullin v Sherlock, 2018 ONCA 1063 (para 55)), outweigh the costs, including possible delays e.g. where a scheduled trial, built on one-party participation, might have to be pushed back to accommodate two-party steps.
In TLA Food Services Ltd. v.
1144707 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 550, 2011 CarswellAlta 1540, 525 A.R.
1, 56 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 363, Justice Shelley discussed the effect of noting a defendant in default.
At paragraphs 18 and 24, Shelly, J. summarized the law: 18 Strekaf J., in Toerper v.
Hoard, 2011 ABQB 85, discussed the effect of a defendant's failure to file a defence under R.
3.37, citing Robinson v.
Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311, 450 AR 167 and McElroy v.
Cowper-Smith, [1967] S.C.R.

These cases, and others cited therein, provide that under the old rules (Alta Reg 390/1968), in Alberta noting in default means that the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim are admitted by the defendant.
(Robinson at para.
11; McElroy at p.
425 (per Hall J.) and 428 (per Spence J.).
Strekaf J. applied these principles to the new Rule.
I agree that these principles continue to apply. … 24 A summary of these principles follows: 1.
When a defendant is noted in default, it is deemed to have admitted the allegations in the Statement of Claim; 2.
Before granting default judgment the Court must still inquire as to whether a cause of action is made out in the Statement of Claim, and may direct a hearing on the matter; 3.
A defendant who has been noted in default cannot adduce evidence to contradict the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim in the course of a hearing for the assessment of damages; 4.
Quantum of damages may be assessed based on affidavit evidence; 5.
R.

152 of the previous rules gives the Chambers judge discretion as to whether to grant default judgment ex parte based on affidavit evidence or to require that notice be given and an assessment set down for hearing.
In Argent v.
Gray, 2015 ABQB 292, a defendant had been noted in default.
However, he would have had a defence under the Limitations Act.

Justice Dario concluded that the defendant could not avail himself of that defence though the Plaintiff could still be required to prove its claim against the defendant: 44 Having been noted in default, Mr.
McMillan cannot avail himself of the limitations defence applicable to the other Defendants.
In Makowichuk v Makowichuk, 2013 ABCA 439, 60 CPC

(7th) 448 at para 9, the Court of Appeal held: • The appellant's position is of course contrary to s 3 of the Limitations Act, the relevant portion of which provides: “the defendant on pleading this Act as a defence, is entitled to immunity from liability in respect of the claim.” In other words, it requires that the defence be pleaded in order to give rise to the immunity.
The logical extension of the appellant's position is that the immunity is available without so pleading, indeed, without even filing the Statement of Defence.
In our opinion, that position is without merit.
45 Nevertheless, given that Rule 3.37 allows a court to dismiss a plaintiff's claim notwithstanding a noting in default, I am satisfied that the Plaintiffs cannot succeed against Mr.
McMillan unless they prove their claim against him ….
Service of Amended Statement of Claim when Defendant Noted in Fault In Clarke v.
Deranger, 2006 ABQB 442, 2006 CarswellAlta 773, 400 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 382, Macklin J. stated, at p.

334: 30 While Rule 144 of the Rules of Court does provide that a defendant “who fails to defend or demand notice is not entitled to notice of any subsequent proceedings in the action,” this can only refer to proceedings that relate to the allegations in the original statement of claim of which the defendant has either received, or been deemed to have received, notice.

I am not prepared to interpret the Rule as having the effect of allowing a plaintiff to proceed against a defendant on new allegations of which the defendant has no knowledge when the defendant has been noted in default of filing a defence to the original statement of claim.

31 A defendant who is served, either personally or substitutionally, with a copy of a statement of claim, may decide not to defend the action because the allegations are true, they are insufficient to make out a case against the defendant, or for some other reason.

However, the defendant's failure to file a defence to a statement of claim does not give the plaintiff carte blanche to amend the claim by adding serious allegations against the defendant which will expose him to liability, where he did not have any before, or increase his potential liability, and then to proceed as though the defendant has admitted those new allegations.
When the Court Doubts There Is a Cause of Action In Dykes v.
Goczan (1996), 38 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 425 (Q.B.), the defendant had been noted in default but sought leave to tender evidence contradicting the facts set forth in the Statement of Claim.
Binder J. dismissed the application, but agreed that leave could be granted if the Court were of the view that the plaintiff did not have a cause of action.
At pp.

353-354, His Lordship said: …[W]hen a defendant is noted in default the legal position in Alberta is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim by the failure to deny them.
There is, however, an exception, which is the basis of the Spiller[Spiller v.
Brown, [1973] 6 W.W.R.
663 (Alta.
C.A.)] decision, that where the court is not satisfied that the plaintiff has a cause of action, the court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter.

In that case for example, the trial judge had a suspicion that the plaintiff was manoeuvring to remove other defendants from the action to avoid the need to prove that the defendant who had not filed a defence was guilty of gross negligence.
When Alternative Remedies Were Sought In TLA Food Services Ltd. v.
1144707 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 550, 2011 CarswellAlta 1540, 525 A.R.
1, 56 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 363, a Plaintiff noted a Defendant in default.
The Statement of Claim sought damages, rectification of the contract in dispute, and specific performance of the contract.
Justice Shelley held that the Defendant was entitled to notice of which remedy the Plaintiff sought, and that an ex parte application for rectification was not appropriate.
At paragraphs 53-54, her Ladyship said: 53 In Fenske v.
Schneider, 2007 ABQB 164, Veit J. held that, where a plaintiff has sought alternative remedies, the defendant should be given notice of a motion by the plaintiff to seek one of those remedies.
Veit J. noted “a default of defence is an admission of the facts pleaded, not of the conclusions of law or the assessment of damages” (at para.
11) and “that the appropriate remedy flowing from that breach is not a fact which [the defendant] can be taken to have admitted” (at para.
In Fenske the plaintiff sought either damages or specific performance in the Statement of Claim, and then sought specific performance in the application for default judgment.
Veit J. refused the application, noting (at paras.

15-16): … not only does the Statement of Claim itself advances two possible remedies, the remedy of specific performance is a discretionary, equitable remedy which will only be granted after a review of all pertinent circumstances.
Mr.
Fenske may well have a strong claim for specific performance: Fossum, [1997] A.J.
No.
No.
1424, United Gulf Developments Ltd., [2004] N.S.J.
No.
66, Spicer, [2005] A.J.
No.
That is not the point.
The issue is that Ms.
Schneider may well have a position concerning the request for specific performance as opposed to a request for damages; she is entitled to advance that position for the court's consideration.
54 Similarly here, TLA's Claim sought damages, rectification of the Contract, and specific performance.
In my view, as in Fenske, notice must be given to the Defendants of TLA's choice of remedy so that they can advance a position in regards to the appropriate equitable remedy.
I conclude that this is a further ground for denying TLA's application.
Effects of Noting in default or Striking of defence In Boyer v.

Boyer, 2024 ABKB 727, Justice Lema discussed the possible effects of having a defence struck, or being noted in default: [52] Most of the no-defendant cases involve defendants noted in default, versus struck-pleadings defendants.
[53] I find that the principles governing noting-in-default cases apply equally to those involving struck pleadings.
[54] In both scenarios, the defendant has, or ends up with, no pleading in opposition to the statement of claim.
[55] In the struck-pleadings scenario, the defendant ends up in the same position as if he, she or it had not defended in the first place.

[56] Technically speaking, the plaintiff in a struck-pleadings scenario could note the defendant in default post-striking; however, that step appears unnecessary, with the striking accomplishing the same thing (no defence, or no more defence).

[57] As I see it, the functional equivalence of the two scenarios is recognized in Rules 3.36 and 3.37, which provide the same consequences and next-step options for the Court and the parties i.e. whether no defence was filed or a defence was struck. … [62] The critical impact of a noting in default or pleading being struck is losing the ability to challenge the facts asserted in the opposing party's pleadings, as explained in the cases below, starting with Robinson v Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311 (Yamauchi J.): The strongest statement on the effect of the Defendants' failure to file a statement of defence was made by the Supreme Court of Canada in McElroy v.
Cowper-Smith, 1967 CanLII 70 (SCC), [1967] S.C.R.
425 at 428, where Spence J. considered the reasoning in Sulef v.
Parkin (1966), 1966 CanLII 638 (AB CA), 57 W.W.R.
236 (Alta.
S.C.- App.
Div.) and said: … in the province of Alberta upon default in defence the defendant is to be taken to have admitted the facts set out in the statement of claim.
This is a decision of the highest court in Alberta on a point of practice in the province, and this court will not interfere under such circumstances.
Therefore, the respondents, as plaintiffs at trial, were not required to prove publication of the alleged libel.

Although Spence J. was writing in dissent, many Alberta cases since that time have held that the effect of a noting in default is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by the failure to deny them, see e.g.
Klinck v.
Drinnan, [1985] A.J.
No.
576 (Q.B.), Dykes v.
Goczan, [1996] A.J.
No.
432 (Q.B.) (“Dykes”); Syncrude Canada Ltd. v.
Tibo Steel Products Ltd., 2001 ABQB 478 (CanLII), [2001] A.
J.
No.
736 (Q.B.); Dyck v.
Wilkinson, 2004 ABQB 731 (CanLII), [2004] A.
J.
No.
More relevant to the case with which this Court is dealing is a statement by Harvey C.J.A. in Brennan v.
Arcadia Coal Co.
(1929), 1929 CanLII 274 (AB CA), 24 Alta.
L.R.

236 at 448 (C.A.) (“Brennan”), where he said: The amount of damages to which the plaintiff was entitled could only be ascertained by an assessment but the evidence to be taken on such assessment would only be for the purpose of ascertaining the amount of, and in no sense the liability for, such damages which latter has been established by the facts alleged and admitted by the defendant by reason of its failure to deny them.

[paras 10-11] [emphasis added] [63] As Yamauchi J. discussed further, the court must be satisfied that the admitted facts add up to a cause of action and that it has jurisdiction to grant the requested relief: The mere noting in default, however, does not end the matter.
In Dykes at para.
6, Binder J., based on Spiller v.
Brown, 1973 ALTASCAD 76 (CanLII), [1973] 6 W.W.R.
663 (Alta.

C.A.) (“Spiller”), said that there is an exception to the rule that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by failure to deny them “where the Court is not satisfied that the Plaintiff has a cause of action, the Court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter.” This Court has reviewed the pleadings filed in this matter and has heard the testimony of Robinson and concludes that the Plaintiffs have a cause of action against the Defendants.
Plaintiffs' counsel argued that the pleadings, proof of service of the pleadings on the Defendants and the praecipe to note in default all provide this Court with jurisdiction to assess damages.
This Court disagrees with that proposition based on the statement by Johnson J.A. in Spiller at para.
8, where he said, “Neither by pleadings nor admissions can a defendant give a court jurisdiction that it does not otherwise have,” see also Muscutt v.
Courcelles (2002), 2002 CanLII 44957 (ON CA), 213 D.L.R.
(5th) 206 at para.
50 (Ont.
C.A.) (“Muscutt”).
Thus, this Court must determine whether it has jurisdiction even in the face of the noting in default.

[paras 12-13] [emphasis added] [64] As confirmed in Smith v Tuchscherer, 2024 ABCA 186: … when proceeding on default or after pleadings are struck, counsel and parties remain obliged to prove entitlement to the remedies sought and to respect the limits of the served pleadings: TLA Food Services Ltd v 1144707 Alberta Ltd, 2011 ABQB 550 [Shelley J.].
[65] Another dimension of participation is applying for relief under the Rules of Court.

In the analogous context of a party being noted in default, the noted-in-default party is still a party for the purpose of “tak[ing] any other step under the Rules”, per Yaremchuk v Haight, 2001 ABCA 7 (considering the pre-2010 Rules): In my view, a party who is noted in default does not cease to be a party to the action and is entitled to utilize Rule 244.1 [dismissal-for-delay rule].
According to Rule 142(3) once a defendant has been noted in default he or she is no longer entitled to deliver a statement of defence or demand of notice.

Furthermore, once the defendant has been noted in default: [a]ll the plaintiff has to prove, or the defendant is permitted to controvert, is the amount of the damages; for the cause of action itself, as stated in the plaintiff's claim, and the right to some damages in respect of it, is admitted by the defendant, by his suffering judgement to pass against him by default.
T.W.
Chitty, ed., Chitty's Archibold's Practice of the Queen's Bench Division, vol.
2, 14th ed.
(London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1885) at 1336, as cited in Sulef v.
Parkin and Breno (1966), 1966 CanLII 638 (AB CA), 57 W.W.R.
236 (Alta.
C.A.) But I have not been provided with any authority or directed to any Rule which might otherwise limit the right of a defendant to take any other step under the Rules.

[para 5] [emphasis added] [66] A noted-in-default party's participation rights (there too to apply to have the remaining party's action struck for delay) were again examined in Zivkovic v Zivkovic, 2009 ABQB 542 (Veit J.).
[67] Zivkovic was decided under the former rules but with an awareness of the proposed new (circa 2010) rules, including Rules 3.36 and 3.37.
[68] After considering Yaremchuk (cited above), Veit J. observed: The approach taken by our Court of Appeal is not the approach taken in other jurisdictions.
For example, the Ontario Rules of Court specifically state that a defendant who is in default cannot ask for dismissal of an action for delay: see Rule 24.01.
However, in Ontario, a defendant who is in default can apply to the court for leave to bring a motion other than a motion to set the default praecipe aside.
While that approach may be more logically consistent, our Court of Appeal has effectively short-circuited the need to make an application to move under R.
244.1 [dismissal for long delay].

[para 31] [emphasis added] [69] She concluded: It appears to me that ALRI's proposed new Rules of Court [i.e. which became the 2010 Rules] do not clarify the issues raised by this motion [i.e. a noted-in-default party's rights]: proposed Rules 3.36(1)(b), R.
4.33 do not appear to give more guidance that is present under the existing Rules.

Given the increasing number of self-represented litigants, especially in family law matters, it might be useful to provide explicit direction to such litigants about, for example, the effect of not defending an action.
[para 37] [emphasis added] [70] I echo Veit J.s comments, finding them equally applicable to a struck-pleadings scenario.
In both scenarios, the 2010 Rules do not explicitly address the effect of a party being noted in default or having its pleadings struck.

While Rules 3.36 and 3.37 (discussed further below) provide various options for the Court in such scenarios, they do not (or at least not expressly) address whether the defendant continues to have any right(s) to participate in the proceeding or, if so, the nature and extent of any such right(s). … [73] On another dimension of participation, a noted-in-default or struck-pleadings party continues to be entitled to copies of orders and judgments affecting them, per Rule 9.8: Unless these rules otherwise provide or the Court otherwise orders, the party who enters the judgment or order must serve a copy of the entered judgment or order on each of the other parties.

[74] The core definition of “party” (Appendix to the Rules of Court) is “a party to an action.” Per Yaremchuk (cited above), a noted-in-default (or, by extension, struck-pleadings) litigant does not cease to be a party (para 5).

[75] On the overall impacts of pleadings being struck, Shelley J. surveyed the Alberta noting-in-default case law (which I find applicable to the struck-pleadings scenario) in TLA Food Services Ltd v 1144707 Alberta Ltd, 2011 ABQB 550, distilling the following principles: 1.
When a defendant is noted in default, it is deemed to have admitted the allegations in the Statement of Claim; 2.
Before granting default judgment the Court must still inquire as to whether a cause of action is made out in the Statement of Claim, and may direct a hearing on the matter; 3.
A defendant who has been noted in default cannot adduce evidence to contradict the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim in the course of a hearing for the assessment of damages; 4.
Quantum of damages may be assessed based on affidavit evidence; 5.
R.

152 of the previous rules gives the Chambers judge discretion as to whether to grant default judgment ex parte based on affidavit evidence or to require that notice be given and an assessment set down for hearing.
[para 24] [emphasis added] [76] For reference, here is former R.

152: If a sole defendant has, or all the defendants have, been noted in default, the plaintiff may: a. apply ex parte to the court for judgment, and the judge hearing the application may i. upon proof of the plaintiff's claim by affidavit or otherwise, give final judgment or direct an accounting, [or] ii. set the matter over for a hearing on notice, and notice shall be given to a defendant in the same manner as hereinafter provided on assessment or b. set the matter down for assessment, giving at least 10 days notice of the date set for the assessment.
[77] Justice Shelley's distillation has been found applicable in the new
(2010) Rules era, as reflected by its endorsement in Smith (ABCA — cited above) and other decisions, including Lund v Quinn Maintenance Inc, 2020 ABQB 722 (Eamon J) (para 8)
Simmer v Copithorne, 2018 ABQB 525 (Eamon J.) (para 6)
Roberts v Safadi, 2018 ABQB 165 (Mandziuk J.) (para 8); and Argent v Gray, 2015 ABQB 292 (Dario J.) (para 45).

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.38:1 Rule 3.38 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.38. 1. When a Plaintiff Can Use R. 3.38 to “Recover” Property In TLA Food Services Ltd. v. 1144707 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 550, 2011 CarswellAlta 1540, 525 A.R. 1, 56 Alta. L.R. (5th) 363, the Plaintiff sued the Defendant for breach of a contract under which the Defendant sold a hotel and its parking lot to the Plaintiff. The relevant facts were summarized in paragraph 1 of the decision: 1 TLA Food Services Ltd. (TLA) entered into a contract (the Contract) with 1144707 Alberta Ltd. (1144707) to purchase a hotel. Unknown to the Plaintiff and to its principal, Tilemachos Tziachris, the hotel and hotel parking lot were located on two parcels. The hotel building is located on both, and the hotel parking lot is situated entirely on one of them. The land description in the Contract did not include the parcel on which the parking lot and part of the building are located. TLA sued 1144707, who did not defend and was noted in default. Justice Shelley dismissed an application to rectify the contract, and then discussed whether the Plaintiff could recover the parking lot land pursuant to R. 3.38. She said, at paragraphs 45–52: 45 However, if I am wrong, and the Contract can be rectified, I will consider whether default judgment can be entered under Rule 3.38 to permit TLA to obtain title to Property 2. 46 Rule 3.38 provides that, when no defence or demand for notice is filed to a claim for recovery of property, the Plaintiff may enter judgment for the recovery of that property. The immediate predecessor of this Rule is R. 149. Neither Rule has been subject to judicial commentary or discussion. Stevenson and Cote, in both the 2009 and 2010 Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook, (Edmonton, Juriliber, 2009 and 2010), have no commentary regarding either version of the Rule. 47 Rule 3.38 adds a parenthetical comment “[When no defence is filed in a foreclosure action]”, which initially seems to suggest that the Rule is applicable only to foreclosure actions. However, that parenthetical comment follows the phrase “Subject to rule 3.41”. Rule 3.41 is entitled “When no defence is filed in a foreclosure action”, and provides that “If a defendant in a foreclosure action does not file a statement of defence or demand for notice, the plaintiff must note the defendant in default before filing an application …” This suggests that the parenthetical reference is to alert the reader to the nature of the “subject to”, rather than to indicate that the Rule applies only to foreclosure actions. On the plain language of the Rule itself, there is no indication that it is so limited. 48 Rule 3.38 provides for “recovery of property”. R. 149 provided for the “recovery of goods or land”. In the successor Rule 3.38 “property” includes both “land and personal property”: Rules of Court, Appendix: Definitions. The plain meaning of “recovery” is to take back something that the Plaintiff previously possessed—to get back or regain something. See Oxford English Dictionary (www.oed.com, July 19, 2011): 4a. The regaining or restoration to one's control or possession of a thing lost, stolen, or otherwise taken away, retrieval; the possibility of recovering such a thing. 49 “Recovery” also has a legal meaning, set out in the Oxford English Dictionary (www.oed.com, July 19, 2011) as: 2a. The fact or process of gaining or regaining possession of or a right to property, compensation, etc., by a legal process or judgment. 50 In my view, this definition is not applicable here. “Recovery” in the latter definition is a general term describing remedies broadly. In that sense, a plaintiff in every action is always seeking recovery for what he asserts he has lost; that recovery may be assessed as damages, specific performance, or some other order. In this context, I find that “recovery of property” references the restoration or regaining of property or title. 51 Moreover, the context of the Rules dealing with default judgment and noting in default further support this interpretation. Rules 3.37, 3.38 and 3.39 provide for two kinds of default judgment—a judgment on application to the Court after a defendant has been noted in default under Rule 3.36. Such a judgment requires an assessment under Rule 3.37. The second form of judgment does not require that a defendant first be noted in default (except in the case of foreclosure (Rule 3.41)) and does not require an application to the Court. These judgments are those for a debt or liquidated demand (Rule 3.39), or “recovery of property” (R. 3.38), and are entered by the plaintiff. 52 In the case of debt or liquidated demand, the jurisprudence has established that such default judgment is only when an exact or easily calculable amount is sued for. Logically, under the similar Rule 3.38, default judgment for the recovery of property should only be available when the property is easily ascertainable, without the need for a Court application. This would be the case in a foreclosure action, where the plaintiff has a mortgage identifying its interest, or in a bailment action, where the plaintiff has an agreement describing the personal property sued for.

These judgments are those for a debt or liquidated demand (Rule 3.39), or “recovery of property” (R.
3.38), and are entered by the plaintiff.
52 In the case of debt or liquidated demand, the jurisprudence has established that such default judgment is only when an exact or easily calculable amount is sued for.
Logically, under the similar Rule 3.38, default judgment for the recovery of property should only be available when the property is easily ascertainable, without the need for a Court application.

This would be the case in a foreclosure action, where the plaintiff has a mortgage identifying its interest, or in a bailment action, where the plaintiff has an agreement describing the personal property sued for.

sentences.text: Judgment for debt or liquidated demand

paragraphs.text: (1) If a statement of claim includes a claim for a debt or a liquidated demand, with or without interest, whether as debt or damages, and one or more defendants do not file a statement of defence or demand for notice in response to that claim or any part of it, the plaintiff (a) may enter judgment for a sum not exceeding the amount in respect of which no defence is filed and the interest payable, if the interest calculation is based on a set rate, either under an agreement or an enactment, and (b) is entitled to a costs award. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.39:1 Rule 3.39 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.39. 1. Interest Section 14(1) of the Judicature Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. J-2 permits the court to award interest “when in the opinion of the Court the payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld and it seems to the Court fair and equitable that the party in default should make compensation by the payment of interest …” 2. Test #1: “Just Debt” … the amount due to be a “just debt” must at least be ascertainable, though not necessarily precisely so, by reference to a contract or agreement between the parties and not as damages. Eyben v. K.R. Ranches (1970) Ltd. (1982), 20 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 at 275 (C.A.). 3. Test #2: “Improperly Withheld” and “Fair and Equitable” Assuming this test [Test #1] to be satisfied, there still remains for decision the question of whether the just debt has been “improperly withheld” and whether it is “fair and equitable that” that interest be paid… In short, there must be something improper about the failure to pay the debt beyond the mere fact that it is due and not paid. So, in the case of one who did not have the means to pay, the failure to pay could hardly be regarded as “improper”. Cases where a failure to pay is nothing more than a deliberate attempt to reap the benefit of high interest rates or to put economic pressure on the creditor so as to induce him to take for immediate payment a sum less than he might otherwise receive may well be regarded as examples of an improper withholding of a just debt and where it is fair and reasonable that the creditor receive appropriate interest. Eyben v. K.R. Ranches (1970) Ltd., supra, at 275. 4. Practice Note (1) That interest should be claimed in the prayer for relief. (2) That in the body of a statement of claim the facts should be pleaded which establish that a just debt has been improperly withheld, giving such particulars as desirable, and that it is fair and equitable that the party in default should make compensation by payment of interest. (3) That it is desirable that the party claiming interest assert the basis for the rate of interest, such as alleging that a certain rate was his cost of borrowing, or, alternatively, that a certain rate was a return that would have been received by him had he been able to invest the money. Eyben v. K.R. Ranches (1970) Ltd., supra, at 275. With respect to (3), remember Kidd J.'s words in Renaissance Resources Ltd. v. Metalore Resources Ltd. (1984), 31 Alta. L.R. (2d) 226 (Q.B.), at 242: It is not sufficient for a plaintiff merely to indicate what bank he uses and what the prime interest rate of the bank is for the period the plaintiff is claiming interest … There must be some evidence of what it cost this plaintiff to borrow and whether he indeed had to borrow. If he did not have to borrow, evidence should be submitted as to the “return that would have been received by him had he been able to invest the money.” 5. Which Forum? For interest under the Judicature Act, one must seek the relief from a judge. That is clearly a claim for interest under s. 15 of the Judicature Act. That kind of claim is an unliquidated damage claim … Masters in Chambers do not have jurisdiction to grant such claims. Elgert Fertilizers Ltd. v. Schmitz (1985), 36 Alta. L.R. (2d) 327 (Master), at 329, per Master Funduk. 6. Implied Abandonment of s. 14 Judicature Act Claim I conclude that when a plaintiff is applying for summary judgment to a master in chambers, where the statement advances a claim for interest under s. 15 [now s. 14], that the plaintiff is abandoning that part of the claim. Elgert Fertilizers Ltd. v. Schmitz, supra, at 330.
