paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.44:1 Rule 3.44 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.44. In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2012 ABQB 679, 2012 CarswellAlta 2257, 549 A.R. 72, 79 Alta. L.R. (5th) 1; [affirmed 2013 ABCA 87] Madam Justice Hughes discussed claims for contribution. At paragraphs 201–205, her Ladyship said: 201 A right to recover contribution arises under statute, specifically under s 3 of the Tort-feasors Act and the Contributory Negligence Act, RSA 2000, c C-27 [the Contributory Negligence Act], and under the common law: MacKay v. Farm Business Consultants Inc, 2006 ABCA 316 at paras 9–12 [MacKay]. 202 The types of third party claims that can be filed under the new Rules include the classic type of third party claims for contribution described under Rule 3.44(a). They now also include third party claims against a party who is or might be liable to the party filing the third party claim for an independent claim (Rule 3.44(b)), or who should be bound by a decision about an issue between the plaintiff and the defendant (Rule 3.44(c)). 1. — Claims for contribution under the common law 203 The Defendants have a right to recover contribution from the Third Parties under the common law, if the Third Parties breached duties they owed directly to the Defendants under contract, tort, statute or otherwise. The right to contribution arises if the damage the Defendants allege they suffered as a result of the Third Parties' breaches are related to the damage that the Plaintiff, CNRL, alleges it suffered as a result of the Defendants' breaches. Because the common law right to contribution arises if the Third Parties breached duties owed directly to the Defendants, it exists independently of any claim that CNRL may have against the Third Parties and can support an independent cause of action against the Third Parties. 204 The nature of the common law claim for contribution, and the distinction between a third party claim for contribution under the common law and under the Tort-feasors Act, was described by Conrad JA in Leoppky at paras 30–33: […] Generally, a defendant may third party a person to enforce a duty or obligation owed by the third party to the defendant which relates to the same damages pled in the statement of claim. For example, where a customer purchases defective goods and sues the vendor, that vendor may be able to third party the manufacturer who supplied the defective goods. That is because the vendor can allege a separate duty owed to it by the manufacturer which could support an independent cause of action giving rise to third party liability. The [defendants] have not alleged any such independent duty or obligation in their third party notice. The facts pled do not disclose any contract, duty of care or statutory obligation owed by [the third party] to the [defendants] which would entitle them to any claim against or contribution from [the third party]. Thus, the third party notice discloses no possible third party liability on [the third party's] part. As noted by this Court in Metz v. Breland (1990), 76 Alta. L.R (2d) 397 (C.A.), a third party notice serves to enforce duties owed by the third party to the defendant, not to enforce duties owed by the third party to the plaintiff. That is the key test which the [defendants] have not met—to demonstrate that there is some duty owed by [the third party] to them […] 205 In the recent decision of Master Schlosser in Pagnucco v. Sears Canada Inc, 2011 ABQB 810 [Pagnucco], a third party claim for contribution was brought under both the Tort-feasors Act and the common law. The Master described the claim for contribution under the common law at para 17: The proposed Third Party Notice has two distinct parts. One part is based on the duties and obligations the proposed Third Party allegedly owed the Defendant. These allegations are pleaded in breach of contract, breach of warranty, negligence and misrepresentation. There is no doubt that these allegations could form the basis of a free standing claim, although the measure of damages might, to a certain extent, relate to the injuries suffered by the Plaintiff. [emphasis added] At paragraphs 241-242; 245 Hughes, J. said: 241 The validity of the third party claims in the Two Actions also depends in part on the types of third party claims that can be made under the Rules. As the Rules have evolved, they have broadened the circumstances under which a party may file a third party claim: see discussion in Dean v. Kociniak, 2001 ABQB 412, 289 AR 201 [Dean]; and the ALRI 2004 Report on Joining Claims and Parties at paras 139–163. 242 The new Rules allow third party claims to enforce claims for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act or the common law, both of which depend upon the success of the plaintiff's claim against the defendant: Rule 3.44(a). The new Rules also allow a third party claim to be filed against a party who is or might be liable to the party filing the third party claim for an independent claim, if the independent claims are related to the matters in the main action (Rule 3.44(b)), and against a party who should be bound by a decision about an issue between the plaintiff and the defendant (Rule 3.44 (c)). … 245 Rule 3.44(a) gives broader rights than former Rule 66(1). Rule 66(1) allowed a defendant to make a third party claim where the defendant claimed against any person “that the person is or may be liable to him for all or part of the plaintiff's claim against him.”[emphasis added]. Rule 3.44(a) now provides that a party may file a third party claim against a person who “is or might be liable to the party filing the third party claim for all or part of the claim against that party”[emphasis added]. As a result, third party claims under Rule 3.44(a) now include both third party claims for contribution arising under the Tort-feasors Act or the common law, the types of third party claims described in paragraphs (1) and (2) of para 123 of the ALRI 2004 Report on Joining Claims and Parties. Justice Hughes provided the following summary regarding third party claims under the common law (at paragraphs 249–251): 249 A claim for contribution under the common law arises when a third party breaches a duty in contract, a common law duty of care or a statutory obligation owed by the third party to the defendant: Leoppky at para 30. 250 Because it is a claim for contribution, it stands or falls based on the outcome of the plaintiff's claim against the defendant. This does not mean that it is derived from the plaintiff's claim against the third party. It does not depend upon the plaintiff having a claim against the third party. A common law claim for contribution is a free-standing claim: Supreme Steel. It arises out of the breach of a separate duty owed by the third party to the defendant “which could support an independent cause of action”: Loeppky at para 30. 251 A third party claim through which a common law claim for contribution is asserted is described as a claim alleging that the “duty or obligation owed by the third party to the defendant … relates to the same damages pled in the statement of claim”[emphasis added]: Leoppky at para 30. A third party claim for contribution under the common law must therefore allege facts that could support a finding that the third party's breach of duty to the defendant caused the defendant to suffer damage that is related to the damage that the plaintiff claims it suffered as a result of the defendant's breach of duty to the plaintiff. And with respect to third party claims for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act, she said at paragraphs 252–258: 252 As is the case with a claim for contribution under the common law, a claim for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act stands or falls based on the outcome of the plaintiff's claim against the defendant. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.45:1 Rule 3.45 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.45. 1. Extension of Time Rule 66 does not provide any guidance as to when the court should or should not extend the time allowed for filing and serving third-party proceedings. I concur with the statement of the Master in Kreway v. Renfrew Chrysler Plymouth et al. and Chrysler Canada Ltd., [1973] 1 W.W.R. 461, where he states that reasons for refusing to extend time are: (1) inordinate delay; (2) absence of credible excuse; and (3) prejudice This decision was subsequently approved by the Alberta Supreme Court, [1973] 1 W.W.R. 462. Edmonton & Rural Auxilliary Hospital & Nursing Home District No. 24 v. Bittorf-Holland-Christianson Architects Ltd. (1981), 33 A.R. 60 at 63 (Q.B.). In a later decision, the Alberta Court of Appeal considered delay as: … a reason for refusing a third party notice where the defendant is alerted by the pleading as to the nature of the claim and the magnitude of the claim against him when he makes his election not to issue a third party notice. That election is made when the time established by the rules expires. E.S.M. Transport Ltd. v. Western Mack Truck (Edmonton) Ltd. (1988), 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 115 at 117 (C.A.). As to when to bring the application: … an order extending time for filing and serving a third party notice should not be made unless there is material filed to support such order. Sheahan v. Fischer (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 300 at 302 (Master). In Lister v. Calgary (City) (1997), 47 Alta. L.R. (3d) 14, the Court of Appeal commented on the need for evidence in support of an application to extend time for filing. At pp. 16-17, the court said: Where a party seeks a significant time extension, it is expected to give evidence to explain the delay, i.e. why prompt compliance did not occur. Maybe it would be different if the extension sought was slight, but here the delay was over four and one-half years. Evidence must be proper admissible evidence such as an affidavit, not mere allegations by counsel. The cases on time extensions generally, and those on later third party notices, seem to agree on those points. . . . . . … the onus of proof is on the City, which is the one which moved for leave to issue a pleading four and one-half years late. The third party is not obliged to lead any evidence at all, let alone evidence which excludes doubt. The onus is on the City to lead evidence which justifies the late pleading by explaining the delay. In Kaptian v. Hardy (1999), 251 A.R. 291 (Q.B.), at p. 295, Chief Justice Moore said: The length of any delay is relevant as it relates to: the reasonableness of an excuse for the delay, prejudice because of the delay, third party procedure benefits. The test can therefore be subsumed into two parts. 1. Reasonable Excuse A defendant has the burden of proof on an application to extend the time limit of rule 66(4). The six month time frame open to a defendant to file a third party notice gives the defendant an opportunity to consider potential third parties. Any delay after the expiry of the six months requires a reasonable excuse. If a defendant has no reasonable excuse for the delay then leave to add a third party will be denied. 2. Prejudice If a defendant has a reasonable excuse for the delay, then the court must balance the potential prejudice to the third party and the plaintiff because of the delay against the benefits of adding the third party. If the prejudice outweighs the benefits of third party procedure, then leave to add a third party will be denied. However, in Flight v. Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211, 2001 CarswellAlta 322, 284 A.R. 117, Madam Justice Moreau disagreed with Chief Justice Moore's requirement that any delay beyond the six-month period requires a reasonable excuse. At p. 126, Her Ladyship said: … I am of the view that the proper test for an application to strike a third party notice is as suggested by the authorities which preceded Kaptian, supra and that prejudice is still a factor to be weighed along with the nature of the delay and whether it can be reasonably excused, unless the delay is significant. In that event, the absence of a reasonable excuse for the delay effectively overpowers any need on the part of the third party to demonstrate actual prejudice. I therefore respectfully disagree with my former colleague that every case of delay beyond the six-month time frame contemplated by rule 66(4) requires the defendant to advance a reasonable excuse before any consideration of prejudice comes into play. I would agree with the approach taken in [Grandwood Flooring Western Ltd. v. Prism Construction Co. and Edson (1986), 43 Alta. L.R. (2d) 337 (Master)], namely that a short delay would result in a different weighing exercise, focusing primarily on the existence of any prejudice. As one moves further away from the six-month deadline, the weighing exercise will focus more on whether the delay is excusable. In the case of a significant delay … failure to advance a reasonable excuse for the delay will, without more, be fatal to an application to extend time. In Dean v. Kociniak, 2001 ABQB 412, 2001 CarswellAlta 709, 289 A.R. 201, 92 Alta. L.R. (3d) 92, Slatter J. said, at p. 223: With respect, I agree with the decision in Flight v. Dillon that the sequential test set out in Kaptian v. Hardy is not inflexible. The length of the delay, the explanation for the delay, and the relative prejudice to the two parties are to be considered concurrently when the Court exercises its discretion to allow or reject a late Third Party claim. Obviously, the longer the delay, the more the Court might assume prejudice from the mere passage of time, as memories will tend to weaken, the litigation will tend to advance further, and the Third Party might increasingly be prejudiced by the passage of time. However, the mere fact that there is no satisfactory explanation for some or all of the delay is not fatal to the application. In Builders Holdings Ltd. v. Gasland Properties Ltd., 2001 ABQB 823, 2001 CarswellAlta 1740, 306 A.R. 163, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 231, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 231, Mr. Justice Lee said, at p. 246: In my opinion, with the exception of Kaptian, the trend of the case law has been to consider all three factors, balancing the length of the delay with the requirement of an explanation and with the absence of prejudice. The longer the delay, the greater the requirement for a reasonable explanation. Prejudice will always be an important factor. In Kwik-Kopy Printing Canada Corp. v. Skoreik (2002), 324 A.R. 126 (Q.B.), at p. 135, Watson J. held that “it is within the jurisdiction of a Court to look at whether there is an air of reality to the foundation of the Third Party Notice in deciding whether to grant leave to file such outside of the time limit.” In Hein v. Barrett (2008), 96 Alta. L.R. (4th) 397 (Master), Master Hanebury summarized the law (at pp. 403-404): 23 From this case law the following principles emerge: 1. Three factors are considered when determining an application to extend the time for filing a third party notice: the length of the delay, the reason for the delay and the prejudice to the third party. 2. Depending on the length of the delay, different weights may be given to the other two factors. 3. For a short period of delay, the primary consideration is prejudice, and an excuse for the delay is of less importance. 4. The relevant importance of these factors is reversed as the length of the delay increases. The longer the delay the greater the importance of an excuse for the delay and the lesser the importance of the question of prejudice. 5. When there is a significant delay, the lack of a reasonable excuse, without more, will be fatal to the application. 6. The pace of the litigation can also be considered when deciding the weight to be assigned to each of the three factors. In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2012 ABQB 679, 2012 CarswellAlta 2257, 549 A.R. 72, 79 Alta. L.R. (5th) 1; [affirmed 2013 ABCA 87] Madam Justice Hughes said, at paragraphs 497–500: 497 Rule 3.45 requires a third party claim to be filed and served within six months of the filing of the statement of defence. This time may be extended after the consideration of the following three factors: (1) the length of delay; (2) the reason for the delay; and (3) the prejudice to the third party: Alliance Pipeline at para 10 citing Flight v. Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211, 284 AR 117 [Flight]; Dean; and Builders Holdings Ltd. v. Gasland Properties, Ltd, 2001 ABCA 823, 306 AR 163. 498 The requirement to explain the delay is mandatory: Mangat v. Allen, 2010 ABQB 264 at para 10. 499 When the delay is relatively short, more weight is given to the existence of prejudice resulting from the delay and less to the length of delay. As the length of the delay becomes longer, more weight is given to the reason for the delay and less to the existence of prejudice: Spartek Systems Inc v. Brown, 2009 ABQB 705 at para 14, 481 AR 213 [Spartek]; Flight; Dean; Alliance Pipeline at para 10. A delay of approximately 10–14 months is considered relatively short: Alliance Pipeline at para 11. When the delay is longer, the defendant seeking the extension must give evidence explaining the delay. Evidence explaining the delay was required in Lister v. Calgary (City) (1997), 193 AR 218 (CA) where the delay was 4.5 years: para 20. Leave will be denied if the delay is long and no evidence is provided to explain it. In Hein v. Barrett, 2008 ABQB 548, leave was refused where an insufficient explanation was given for a seven-year delay. The pace of the litigation is another factor to be considered in weighing the three factors: Spartek at para 14. 500 The viability of the proposed third party claim will be considered when determining whether an extension of time to file the third party claim should be granted. The claim must have an “air of reality”: LaBell v. Jo (R) (1990), 105 AR 319 at para. 4. In Nelson & Nelson v. Condominium Corporation No. 0013187, 2019 ABQB 426, 2019 CarswellAlta 1148, 93 C.C.L.I. (5th) 344, Justice Hollins said: [49] The 6-month time period in Rule 3.45 can be extended in the discretion of the Court; Rule 13.5. In the absence of an agreement to extend that time, a defendant can apply for an extension of time to add a third party. However, that defendant must show that the delay in applying to add the third party has not been inordinate, that there is a credible excuse for the delay and that the late addition of a third party will not cause prejudice; Condominium Plan 9812082 v Battistella Developments Inc, 2014 ABQB 644 (CanLII) at para.15. … [51] As (now Chief) Justice Moreau explained in Flight v Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211 (CanLII) at para.29, where the delay is short, the focus will be less on the excuse offered for the delay than on the potential prejudice. Where the delay is longer, the prejudice may be assumed and the excuse for the delay becomes more important. Where there has been significant delay, a reasonable excuse must be provided.

Three factors are considered when determining an application to extend the time for filing a third party notice: the length of the delay, the reason for the delay and the prejudice to the third party.
Depending on the length of the delay, different weights may be given to the other two factors.
For a short period of delay, the primary consideration is prejudice, and an excuse for the delay is of less importance.
The relevant importance of these factors is reversed as the length of the delay increases.
The longer the delay the greater the importance of an excuse for the delay and the lesser the importance of the question of prejudice.
When there is a significant delay, the lack of a reasonable excuse, without more, will be fatal to the application.
The pace of the litigation can also be considered when deciding the weight to be assigned to each of the three factors.
In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v.
Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2012 ABQB 679, 2012 CarswellAlta 2257, 549 A.R.
72, 79 Alta.
L.R.

(5th) 1; [affirmed 2013 ABCA 87] Madam Justice Hughes said, at paragraphs 497–500: 497 Rule 3.45 requires a third party claim to be filed and served within six months of the filing of the statement of defence.

This time may be extended after the consideration of the following three factors: (1) the length of delay; (2) the reason for the delay; and (3) the prejudice to the third party: Alliance Pipeline at para 10 citing Flight v.
Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211, 284 AR 117 [Flight]; Dean; and Builders Holdings Ltd. v.
Gasland Properties, Ltd, 2001 ABCA 823, 306 AR 163.
498 The requirement to explain the delay is mandatory: Mangat v.
Allen, 2010 ABQB 264 at para 10.
499 When the delay is relatively short, more weight is given to the existence of prejudice resulting from the delay and less to the length of delay.
As the length of the delay becomes longer, more weight is given to the reason for the delay and less to the existence of prejudice: Spartek Systems Inc v.
Brown, 2009 ABQB 705 at para 14, 481 AR 213 [Spartek]; Flight; Dean; Alliance Pipeline at para 10.
A delay of approximately 10–14 months is considered relatively short: Alliance Pipeline at para 11.
When the delay is longer, the defendant seeking the extension must give evidence explaining the delay.
Evidence explaining the delay was required in Lister v.
Calgary (City) (1997), 193 AR 218 (CA) where the delay was 4.5 years: para 20.
Leave will be denied if the delay is long and no evidence is provided to explain it.
In Hein v.
Barrett, 2008 ABQB 548, leave was refused where an insufficient explanation was given for a seven-year delay.
The pace of the litigation is another factor to be considered in weighing the three factors: Spartek at para 14.
500 The viability of the proposed third party claim will be considered when determining whether an extension of time to file the third party claim should be granted.
The claim must have an “air of reality”: LaBell v.
Jo (R) (1990), 105 AR 319 at para.
In Nelson & Nelson v.
Condominium Corporation No.
(5th) 344, Justice Hollins said: [49] The 6-month time period in Rule 3.45 can be extended in the discretion of the Court; Rule 13.5.
In the absence of an agreement to extend that time, a defendant can apply for an extension of time to add a third party.

However, that defendant must show that the delay in applying to add the third party has not been inordinate, that there is a credible excuse for the delay and that the late addition of a third party will not cause prejudice

Condominium Plan 9812082 v Battistella Developments Inc, 2014 ABQB 644 (CanLII) at para.15. … [51] As (now Chief) Justice Moreau explained in Flight v Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211 (CanLII) at para.29, where the delay is short, the focus will be less on the excuse offered for the delay than on the potential prejudice.
Where the delay is longer, the prejudice may be assumed and the excuse for the delay becomes more important.
Where there has been significant delay, a reasonable excuse must be provided.

sentences.text: Third party defendant becomes party

paragraphs.text: (1) On service of a third party claim, (a) the third party defendant becomes a party to the action between the plaintiff and the defendant, and (b) all subsequent proceedings in the action must name the third party as a party in the action between the plaintiff and the defendant. (2) The pleadings between (a) the defendant and the third party defendant, and (b) a third party plaintiff and a third party defendant, form part of the court file between the plaintiff and the defendant. (3) A third party claim must be tried with the other claims in the action unless the Court otherwise orders under rule 3.71.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.46:1 Rule 3.46 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.46. 1. Pierringer Agreement In Canadian Natural Resources Limited v. Wood Group Mustang (Canada) Inc. (IMV Projects Inc.), 2018 ABCA 305, 2018 CarswellAlta 2079, Justice Slatter explained Pierringer agreements and compared them to Mary Carter agreements: 119 In the month immediately before the trial, CNRL entered into Pierringer settlement agreements with Shaw Pipe and Flint Field Services. Under a Pierringer agreement, the plaintiff enters into final settlements with some of the defendants, who withdraw from the litigation. The plaintiff then proceeds to trial against the non-settling defendants: Pierringer v Hoger, 124 NW 2d 106 (1963 SC Wisconsin). The settling defendants agree to pay a sum of money, they are no longer parties to the action, and the plaintiff agrees not to pursue the non-settling defendants for more than their proportionate liability. Since the non-settling defendants cannot be liable for more than their proportionate share of the damage, the settling defendants are not exposed to any claim for contribution from the non-settling defendants. 120 There are many variations of partial settlement agreements: CCS Corp. v Secure Energy Services Inc., 2016 ABQB 94 at para. 32, 83 CPC (7th) 126. Pierringer agreements can be contrasted with another common type, Mary Carter agreements: Booth v Mary Carter Paint Co., 202 So 2d 8 (1967 Fl Dist CA). In a Mary Carter agreement, the plaintiff is guaranteed a fixed recovery from the settling defendants, but the settling defendants remain parties to the action and seek to maximize recovery from the non-settling defendants. The settling defendants' exposure is capped at the agreed amount, but the settling defendants' obligation decreases in direct proportion to any increase in the non-settling defendants' liability as determined at trial. Justice Slatter then made this observation about Pierringer agreements (at paragraphs 125 and 127): [125]… the existing rule in Bedard v. Amin[2010 ABCA 3], which provides that the plaintiff must account to the non-settling defendants if it “over settled”. In other words, if a settling defendant agrees to pay the plaintiff more than the trial judge finds that settling defendant would have been liable for, the non-settling defendant is entitled to credit for that “overpayment” in order to avoid the plaintiff being double compensated. … … [127]… The effect of Bedard v. Amin is that the risk of a Pierringer settlement falls on the plaintiff. If the plaintiff “under-recovers” from the settling defendants, it will not be able to make up that shortfall from the non-settling defendants. On the other hand, if the plaintiff “over-recovers” from the settling defendants (as in Bedard v. Amin) it will not be allowed to keep the surplus. The Court declined to overrule Bedard v. Amin (see paragraph 148). In Slaferek v. TCG International Inc. (1997), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 279 (Q.B.), Clarke J. explained a Pierringer agreement. The plaintiffs commenced an action against the defendants who brought third parties into the action. The plaintiff ultimately settled with the third parties (referred to by Clarke J. as “the other third parties”). That settlement agreement contained terms which limited the liability of the other third parties in the both the main action and the contribution and indemnity proceedings (the settlement amount), and further obligated the plaintiff to indemnify the other third parties for any amount in excess of the settlement amount ultimately found owing to the plaintiff or the defendants by the other third parties. The other third parties successfully sought from Clarke J. an order striking out the third party notice. In the course of deciding to strike the third party notice, Clarke J. said, at pp. 285-86: Finally, the Other Third Parties describe the nature of their arrangement with the Plaintiff Darin Slaferek as a Pierringer agreement. In that regard, they were referring to the case of Pierringer v. Hoger (1963), 124 N.W. 2d 106 in the Supreme Court of Wisconsin. That case involved an action arising out of an explosion wherein the settling tort feasors moved for summary judgment to dismiss cross-complaints of non-settling tort feasors for contribution. At pp. 111-112 the Court had this to say: … The issue between the plaintiff and the non-settling defendant which should be framed by an amendment to the pleadings is the percentage of causal negligence, if any, of the non-settling defendant, but such percentage of negligence can only be determined by a proper allocation of all of the causal negligence, if any, of all the joint feasors and of the plaintiff if contributory negligence is involved. The determination of this issue between the plaintiff and the non-settling defendant does not require the settling defendants to remain parties because the allocation, if any, of the casual negligence of the settling tort feasors is merely a part of the mechanics by which the percentage of causal negligence of the non-settling tort feasors is determined. It makes no practical difference to the settling tort feasors what percentage of casual negligence is allocated to them because they have bought their peace in any event… Upon the trial the release should be given immediate effect as it is for contribution purposes and the judgment if any against the non-settling defendants should only be for that percentage of negligence allocated to him by the findings or the verdict. The claim for the balance has been satisfied by the plaintiff and there is no point going through this circuitry of ordering a judgment for a larger amount and requiring the plaintiff to satisfy it… The objectives of a Pierringer agreement for the Other Third Parties of course are to set a limit upon their liability and to reduce the cost in terms of both money and personnel involved in litigating the matter. The objective for the administration of justice is to focus the issues the Court will be required to deal with to a determination of what negligence if any can the Plaintiff Darin Slaferek bring home to Calido [the defendant] and if so what percentage of overall negligence should be borne by Calido. The end result should be a shorter and more efficient trial. All of these objectives in my view are ones that this Court should encourage. Mr. Justice Langston discussed Pierringer agreements, and Mary Carter agreements in Vandevelde v. Smith (1999), 243 A.R. 161 (Q.B.). At p. 164, His Lordship said: The position adopted by the court in Pierringer… is consistent with the view that such agreements limit the liability of the nonsettling defendants to a question of their own several liability. It would appear that the nonsettling defendants do not run the risk of joint liability with the settling parties, since this fact is effectively precluded by the nature of the agreement. Langston J. then specifically commented on Slaferek v. TCG International Inc. (1997), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 279 (Q.B.). At pp. 166-67, he said: In my view Slaferek does not stand for the principle that a nonsettling defendant is precluded from third party action as against a settling defendant because of the provisions of a Pierringer agreement. In Slaferek the plaintiff was proceeding only as against the nonsettling defendant, for its separate individual negligence. It is clear that since the plaintiff had satisfied its claim with the settlors there was no issue of contribution. In Slaferek the court commented on the affect of a Pierringer agreement and suggested that such agreements would focus the issues which the court will be required to deal with and those issues were the determination of what negligence if any can the plaintiff bring home to the remaining defendant, and if so, what percentage of the overall negligence should be born by the remaining defendant. Efforts by one of several tortfeasors to settle with a plaintiff have seen the evolution of two types of agreements, one is the Pierringer agreement the other is termed a “Mary Carter” Agreement which is based on the Florida case of Booth v. Mary Carter Paint Co. (1967), 202 So.2d 8 (Fla. App.). In a Mary Carter agreement the settlor guarantees that the plaintiff will recover a sum certain and it thereby limits its own exposure. The settlor's liability is reduced in proportion to any increase in the nonsettling defendants' liability. The settlor remains a party to the action and may even actively help the plaintiff in its efforts to maximize the damages against the nonsettlors. While the two types of agreements are similar in that they are settlement agreements between a plaintiff and one of several joint tortfeasors, they differ in that under a Pierringer agreement the settling defendant is no longer a party to the action and it is implicit in the agreement that the plaintiff will not pursue the nonsettling defendants for that portion, if any, of liability assessed by the trial judge against the settling party. The settlor gains the advantage of having his liability fixed and therefore not running the risk of paying one hundred (100%) per cent of any joint and several judgment. The issue which remains, and is central to this application is the impact which a Pierringer agreement may have on third party proceedings. The agreement is a contract made after the commencement of litigation to which the nonsettlors are not a party but which may affect their rights adversely. The nature of the agreement, and its timing, may effectively preclude discovery of the settlors and this would affect the nonsettlor's ability to establish negligence on the part of the settling parties. As with a Mary Carter agreement the settling party may be actively engaged in assisting the plaintiff in its efforts to maximize the percentage of liability attributed to the nonsettling party. A review of the decisions in Pierringer and Slaferek clearly suggest that the essence of a Pierringer agreement is the elimination of the settling parties' involvement in the litigation. The result in both cases was the elimination of third party participation in the proceedings. While it is clear that the defendants are not a party to the Pierringer agreements, it is equally clear that their rights may be directly affected by the obligations created in the Pierringer agreements. The means by which third parties were eliminated in both Pierringer and Slaferek illustrates this point. In each case the plaintiff restricted its action to the several liability of the nonsettling defendant. In each case there were provisions for indemnifying the settling parties. The consequence of the plaintiffs' actions was that the third parties were not exposed to any liability either from the plaintiff nor from third party actions. Applications to strike the third party proceedings would not affect the position of the remaining parties and would clarify the issue before the courts. Thus in a circuitous, but effective manner, the plaintiff can arbitrarily affect a nonsettling defendant's rights by completely shielding a third party's exposure. This is clearly in keeping with the intent of Pierringer agreements and this has been the result in cases where Pierringer agreements have been utilized. There is nothing sinister in this process since, at the end of the day, the nonsettling defendant need only address his several liability. However the one real handicap which a nonsettling defendant faces is the issue of the manner in which he is able to prove the degree of his several negligence as it relates to the several negligence of the settling party. Depending upon the timing of the Pierringer agreement the nonsettling defendant may be placed in the position that it is unable to discover a third party who is hastily withdrawn from the proceedings. This issue however, is not unlike situations frequently encountered in litigation where parties may be handicapped in their ability to fully bring forth information which they view as being favourable. The application to amend, as presently advanced by the plaintiff, purports to rely on the Pierringer agreements entered into between the plaintiff and the settling defendants. A review of those agreements does not disclose a requirement for such an application by the plaintiff. A review of the circumstances surrounding this application does not suggest that amending the pleadings as proposed by the plaintiff would in any way clarify the issues with which a trial court must deal. Striking the names of the settling defendants and striking references to their potential liability is not particularly efficacious since those parties remain as litigants by virtue of their third party status. In my view it is proper for the trial judge to have a full understanding of the complexities of the litigation, particularly in view of the fact that he may well have to deal with the apportionment of liability. The agreements, through those portions which do require the plaintiff to make amendments, may well affect the nonsettling defendant's ability to deal with the conduct of their defence. A partial amendment at this juncture, in my view, may well prejudice the defendants' position. The plaintiff is clearly entitled to discontinue as against parties named in a Statement of Claim. Such a discontinuance does not necessarily mandate that there need be an amendment to the pleadings. Courts frequently deal with such situations and the fact that individuals identified in pleadings are no longer parties to the action does not necessarily impact upon the proceedings. In Amoco Canada Petroleum Co. v. Propak Systems Ltd., 1999 ABQB 716, 1999 CarswellAlta 891, 74 Alta. L.R. (3d) 194; affirmed 2001 ABCA 110, 2001 CarswellAlta 575, 281 A.R. 185, 91 Alta. L.R. (3d) 13; leave to appeal refused 2002 CarswellAlta 522, 2002 CarswellAlta 523, 312 A.R. 398 (note) (S.C.C.), at pp. 196-97 [Alta. L.R.], Hart J. gave the following explanation of a Pierringer agreement: The type of settlement agreement reached by the settling parties in this case apparently originated in the case of Pierringer v. Hoger, 124 N.W. 2d 106 (U.S. Wis. S.C. 1963), a decision of the Supreme Court of Wisconsin in October of 1963. In Hudson Bay Mining & Smelting Co. v. Fluor Daniel Wright (1997), 120 Man. R. (2d) 214 (Man. Q.B.), the Manitoba Court of Queen's Bench identified the essential features of a Pierringer Agreement at page 222 to be (a) segregation of the contracting defendant's liability; (b) satisfaction of the contracting defendant's liability to the credit of all parties to the litigation; (c) the plaintiff's ability to continue with the action against the remaining defendants; (d) the plaintiff's agreement that it will indemnify the contracting defendant for any contribution it pays to the other defendants and covenants to satisfy any judgment against the contracting defendant. This case was followed by Rooke J. in Wright (Next Friend of) v. VIA Rail Canada Inc. (2000), 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 166 at 171 (Q.B.). The Court of Appeal reviewed Hart J.'s decision in Amoco Canada Petroleum Co. v. Propak Systems Ltd., 1999 ABQB 716, 1999 CarswellAlta 891, 74 Alta. L.R. (3d) 194; affirmed 2001 ABCA 110, 2001 CarswellAlta 575, 281 A.R. 185, 91 Alta. L.R. (3d) 13; leave to appeal refused 2002 CarswellAlta 522, 2002 CarswellAlta 523, 312 A.R. 398 (note) (S.C.C.), and Fruman J.A. gave the following explanation of what she called “proportionate share settlement agreements”, their effect on discovery rights, and the factors to be considered by the courts that review them (at pp. 190-196): Now past is the day when “settlement agreement” can be understood to refer solely to the final resolution of all outstanding issues between all parties to a lawsuit, effectively bringing the suit to an end. In the last several years, in response to increasingly complex and commensurately dilatory and costly litigation, a new generation of settlement agreements has been cautiously adopted by the litigation bar. The new settlement agreements, which include such exotically named species as the Mary Carter agreement and the Pierringer agreement, endeavour to attain a more limited objective: rather than trying to resolve all outstanding issues among all parties, a difficult task in complicated suits, they aim to manage proactively the risk associated with litigation. In short, contracting litigants prefer the certainty of settlement to the uncertainty and expense of a trial and the possibility of an undesirable outcome. This “risk-management” objective is accomplished by settling issues of liability between some but not all of the parties, thereby reducing the number of issues in dispute, simplifying the action, and expediting the suit. Ancillary benefits include a reduction in the financial and opportunity costs associated with complex, protracted litigation, as well as savings of court time and resources. To the extent that a proportionate share settlement agreement completely removes the settling defendants from the suit, it is like a conventional settlement agreement that brings all outstanding issues between the settling parties to a conclusion. Proportionate share settlement agreements therefore typically include the following elements: 1. The plaintiff receives a payment from the settling defendants in full satisfaction of the plaintiff's claim against them; 2. In return, the settling defendants receive from the plaintiff a promise to discontinue proceedings, effectively removing the settling defendants from the suit; 3. Subsequent amendments to the pleadings formally remove the settling defendants from the suit; and 4. The plaintiff then continues its suit against the non-settling defendants. There is, however, an added complication that a proportionate share settlement agreement must address. As a result of third party proceedings, settling defendants are almost always subject to claims for contribution and indemnity from non-settling defendants for the amount of the plaintiff's loss alleged to be attributable to the fault of the settling defendants. Before the settling defendants can be released from the suit, some provision must be made to satisfy these claims. This obstacle is overcome by including an indemnity clause in which the plaintiff covenants to indemnify the settling defendants for any portion of the damages that a court may determine to be attributable to their fault and for which the non-settling defendants would otherwise be liable due to the principle of joint and several liability. Alternatively, the plaintiff may covenant not to pursue the non-settling defendants for that portion of the liability that a court may determine to be attributable to the fault of the settling defendants. It is the latter approach that prevails in the agreement at issue in this suit, but in either case the goal of the proportionate share settlement agreement is to limit the liability of the non-settling party to its several liability. The Competing Positions This court recently considered the validity of a ‘new generation’ settlement agreement in Margetts v. Timmer Estate, [1997] 1 W.W.R. 25, 192 A.R. 42 (Q.B.); affd. (1999), 244 A.R. 114, 209 W.A.C. 114, 178 D.L.R. (4th) 577 (C.A.) There, the trial court recognized and this court affirmed that a tortfeasor has a legitimate and “undoubted right to contract to minimize his financial exposure to the plaintiffs”: at W.W.R. 39. However, in Margetts, supra, the settlement was in the nature of a Mary Carter agreement, which did not completely remove the settling defendants from the suit. As the settling parties continued to be adversarial in interest, a non-settling party remained entitled to full pretrial disclosure from them. In Margetts, therefore, the court did not need to reconcile settlement rights with a non-settling defendant's ability to exercise its pretrial procedural rights in an effort to deflect the plaintiff's accusation of fault. In addition to being grounded in fundamental principles of justice and framed in the Alberta Rules of Court, a non-settling defendant's ability to defend against a suit is anchored in the statutory requirement found in s. 2(1) of the Contributory Negligence Act: 2. (1) When damage or loss has been caused by the fault of 2 or more persons, the court shall determine the degree in which each person was at fault. The effect of this provision is to compel the court to determine the degrees of fault of all contributors to the plaintiffs' damage, whether or not they currently are or ever have been parties to the action. In effect, this provision acts as a safeguard to establish the proportionate share of each defendant's liability, whether settling or non-settling. It therefore becomes apparent that the right to settle, fixing a settling defendant's financial liability to the plaintiff through contract, may have a direct effect on a non-settling defendant's pretrial rights of discovery and production of documents in order to gather evidence to defend the lawsuit. The B.C. Ferry Approach The Canadian cases in which proportionate share settlement agreements have been considered attempt to balance the right to settle against the right to pretrial disclosure. One approach is represented by the decision of the British Columbia Court of Appeal in British Columbia Ferry Corp. v. T & N plc (1995), 65 B.C.A.C. 118, 106 W.A.C. 118, 27 C.C.L.T. (2d) 287 (C.A.). There, the court decided that the non-settling defendants could not maintain a claim for contribution or indemnity against third parties that had settled with the plaintiffs, pursuant to the terms of a proportionate share settlement agreement. However, the court allowed the non-settling defendants to maintain a claim for a declaration to determine the degree to which the plaintiff's damages were attributable to the settling defendants. The court therefore permitted the action for declaratory relief to remain, keeping the settling defendants in the lawsuit for the purely procedural purpose of allowing the non-settling parties access to pretrial procedural rights. The court concluded that the non-settling defendants would be prejudiced in establishing the fault of the third parties, and thus in maintaining their own defence, if they did not retain the benefit of full pretrial procedural rights against the settling parties: at 302. The decision is based on the proposition that it would be “manifestly wrong if a private accord between plaintiff and third party could work to deprive a defendant of the ability to establish an element of proof essential to a just resolution of the action”: at p. 302 (emphasis added). The difficulty with the B.C. Ferry approach is its emphasis on the potential prejudice a non-settling party might suffer. Indeed, it is likely that a non-settling party will always be able to allege some possible disadvantage when it remains as the sole target for liability after other parties abandon the litigation. That is true whether a partial settlement occurs during the course of litigation or even before an action is launched. The B.C. Ferry approach would seem to permit an action for declaratory relief to be maintained for purely procedural purposes against anyone who settled, whether or not they were ever a named party to the litigation, and even though there were no possibility that they might be liable. Litigation, including settlement, is all about advantage, and corresponding disadvantage or prejudice. Settlement, after all, is nothing more than a compromise, in which parties gamble by trading prospective rights for certainty. Nor does prejudice run in only one direction. Failure to allow settlement by parties who want an exit ramp from costly and prolonged litigation may give a party who refuses to settle an even stronger tactical advantage. An unreasonable party can hold the other parties at ransom, virtually dictating the terms of settlement. It is argued that without complete pretrial disclosure a court will be unable to properly apportion the loss. This argument cuts both ways. The plaintiff always bears the burden of proof at trial. By agreeing to remove the settling defendants from the suit and focussing only on the non-settling defendant's alleged misdeeds, a plaintiff runs the risk of no recovery at trial, for it may fail to prove any basis on which a trial court could assign liability to the non-settling party. Decisions to settle with some but not all defendants give rise to challenging issues. What use can be made by the non-settling defendant of settling defendants' discoveries? Will adverse inferences be drawn against the plaintiff if it does not call settling defendants as witnesses? A plaintiff may encounter considerable obstacles in its attempt to recover any damages. It by no means follows that as a result of a partial settlement the non-settling defendant will shoulder a greater portion of the liability than it ought. The B.C. Ferry approach undervalues the importance of settlement. In these days of spiralling litigation costs, increasingly complex cases and scarce judicial resources, settlement is critical to the administration of justice. … Alberta courts have grappled with the B.C. Ferry approach, attempting to balance the certain benefit of settlement against the potential problem of prejudice. Faced with the difficulty of predicting future prejudice, they have looked to the past, assessing such things as the age and complexity of the action; the number of parties involved; how long the present structure of defendants and third parties has been in place; at what stage in the proceedings the application was made; whether discoveries have taken place, documents been produced and expert reports exchanged; whether a trial date has been set; delays and the reason for them; and whether the non-settling party has diligently exercised discovery rights. See Slaferek, supra; Viridian Inc. v. Dresser Canada Inc. (1999), 247 A.R. 23, 73 Alta. L.R. (3d) 348 at p. 363 (Q.B.); Vandevelde v. Smith (1999), 243 A.R. 161 (Q.B.); and Wright, supra. Generally, the longer the action has been in existence and the greater the pretrial disclosure received by the non-settling defendant, the less likely an Alberta judge will find potential prejudice and the more likely the settlement agreement will be given effect…. Indeed, that approach was followed in the present case. The case management judge concluded that because Propak had the advantage of significant oral examination and discovery of documents, it was “clearly better off” than if the settling parties had not been sued or had been formally released by the plaintiffs from the outset, and would not “in any way” be disadvantaged or prejudiced (AB I at 105). This approach has a number of flaws. First, the analysis tends to be superficial and the conclusions unpersuasive. From a pretrial disclosure point of view, most parties will be better off at a more advanced stage in the litigation process. But a non-settling party, although better off, could still be disadvantaged if a court were to truncate its pretrial procedural rights by giving effect to a proportionate share settlement agreement. No matter how dilatory the defendant has been, no matter how interminable its efforts to mine for information, the potential always exists for the next discovery question it asks to be the one that blows the litigation apart. It is difficult for any judge to definitively conclude that there is no potential for prejudice. A second flaw is that this approach always favours settlement at advanced stages rather than earlier stages of litigation. But public policy dictates otherwise. Early settlement means reduced legal costs and less strain on the court system. In modern, complex litigation, it is the pretrial skirmishes that consume most of the court's calendar. … A third flaw is that it gives little guidance to judges, and creates uncertainty for litigants. Because courts are looking at potential rather than actual prejudice, they sometimes have a difficult time evaluating the competing positions. … A test which institutionalizes this degree of uncertainty is no test at all. By properly drafting a proportionate share settlement agreement, settling parties can ensure that a non-settling defendant is responsible only for its proportionate share of the loss. But a non-settling defendant can always assert some form of potential prejudice, which settling parties cannot avoid by contractual means. Litigants will no doubt be reluctant to spend time evaluating their legal position and displaying their hand in settlement negotiations if there is little ability to predict whether a proportionate share settlement agreement will be given effect by the court. The fundamental problem with the current approach is that it requires judges to balance two competing interests, but gives judges few tools with which to do so. The Alberta Rules of Court contain no express rule permitting third party discovery and at least to this point, no one has come up with a creative way of achieving equivalent disclosure by practice note, statute or private agreement. … Alberta's current pretrial disclosure regime severely restricts third party discovery rights. This limitation, which affects all litigants equally, should not be equated to prejudice. Nor should it be used to justify jettisoning proportionate share settlement agreements in this province. A better solution is to introduce some form of third party discovery in Alberta, to address the type of procedural complaints levied in this case. The fact that non-settling defendants are confined to a statutory disclosure regime constrained by the Alberta Rules of Court is not a proper basis for refusing to give effect to proportionate share settlement agreements. It is one thing when the Alberta Rules of Court limit rights of pretrial disclosure. It is another matter entirely when settling parties deliberately thwart a non-settling party's ability to get at the truth. Courts need not countenance agreements containing express provisions that narrow the procedural rights a non-settling defendant would otherwise have or create other obstacles, for example, prohibiting a settling party from cooperating with a non-settling party, participating in interviews, or voluntarily making documents available. A proportionate share settlement agreement should be disclosed to the non-settling party: Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Co. v. Wright, [1997] 10 W.W.R. 622, 120 Man. R. (2d) 214 (Q.B.); affd. (1998), 131 Man. R. (2d) 133, 187 W.A.C. 133 (C.A.). To ensure that the trial judge is aware of the circumstances under which the non-settling defendant has operated, the terms of the agreement, although not necessarily the amount of the settlement, should also be disclosed to the court. Summary In summary, in evaluating proportionate share settlement agreements: 1. A court must keep in mind the strong public policy reason which encourages settlement; 2. The fact that a non-settling defendant has restricted rights of third party disclosure under the Alberta Rules of Court does not justify refusing to give effect to a proportionate share settlement agreement; 3. A court need not approve a proportionate share settlement agreement containing contractual provisions that directly limit the procedural rights a non-settling defendant would otherwise have; and 4. A proportionate share settlement agreement should be disclosed to the non-settling party. To further reduce potential prejudice, the terms of the agreement, although not necessarily the amount of the settlement, should also be disclosed to the court. Her Ladyship then discussed claims for contribution and claims for indemnity, and their relationship to proportionate share settlement agreements. At pp. 196-197, she said: Some confusion exists about claims for contribution and claims for indemnity. Although it is common practice for multiple defendants to issue cross-claims against one another seeking “contribution and indemnity” in respect of the plaintiff's loss, a claim for contribution is usually based on s. 2 of the Contributory Negligence Act and s. 3 of the Tort-feasors Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. T-6. The combined effect of these statutory provisions is the creation of joint and several liability, whereby a plaintiff may claim the whole of its loss from any one defendant, and that defendant may in turn claim contribution from the other defendants in proportion to their respective degree of fault. In contrast to the statutory basis for a claim for contribution, a claim for indemnity is grounded in either contract or tort, arising from an independent duty of care that one defendant or third party owed to another. Proportionate share settlement agreements are relatively straightforward when all defendants are potentially liable to the plaintiff. A settlement is proper so long as the non-settling defendant's liability is strictly limited to the loss it actually caused. The situation is more complicated when the non-settling defendant has issued a third party notice claiming an independent duty that is owed to it, but not to the plaintiff. A settlement cannot extinguish the non-settling defendant's entitlement to indemnification from the third party unless it also extinguishes the non-settling defendant's liability to the plaintiff in respect of claims for which it could seek indemnification from the third party. In Wright (Next Friend of) v. VIA Rail Canada Inc. (2000), 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 166 at 171 (Q.B.), Rooke J. held, at p. 173, that generally “a true Pierringer agreement should result in the amendment of a Statement of Claim and the striking out of a Third Party Notice to exclude the settling defendant.” His Lordship did discuss possible methods of keeping alive the third party proceedings against the settling defendant so as to permit examination for discovery. However, the parties did not wish him to pursue that course of action, so he did not, though His Lordship's comments at pp. 170-71 may be of some interest to future litigants. With respect to the loss of discovery opportunities resulting from the other parties entering into a Pierringer agreement, at p. 177, Rooke J. gave the following warning to litigants: … it seems that the message must go out to such litigants and counsel on their behalf that, if they do not want to take a chance that a co-defendant/third party will settle with the plaintiff and thereby prohibit them from obtaining necessary discovery, they should be diligent in filing Notices to Co-Defendants, Notices to Third Parties, and in obtaining discovery or other procedures of such co-defendant or third parties at the earliest possible opportunity. In Wright (Next Friend of) v. VIA Rail Canada Inc. (2000), 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 166 at 171 (Q.B.), Rooke J. also addressed the concerns which had been raised by Langston J. in Vandevelde v. Smith (1999), 243 A.R. 161 (Q.B.). At p. 176, His Lordship said: With respect, the answer to these concerns, which appear to relate to real or apprehended inappropriate conduct on the settling parties to take advantage of the non-settling party, is that even in those situations … the Court's discretion remains, as exercised by Langston and Burrows JJ., to dismiss the applications to strike the third party proceedings. In such situations, the result would be that the third party might, for that reason, be required to absorb (at least in the first instance), but for no benefit to itself, the costs involved in remaining a party to the action.

Reg.
Pierringer Agreement In Canadian Natural Resources Limited v.
Wood Group Mustang (Canada) Inc.

(IMV Projects Inc.), 2018 ABCA 305, 2018 CarswellAlta 2079, Justice Slatter explained Pierringer agreements and compared them to Mary Carter agreements: 119 In the month immediately before the trial, CNRL entered into Pierringer settlement agreements with Shaw Pipe and Flint Field Services.
Under a Pierringer agreement, the plaintiff enters into final settlements with some of the defendants, who withdraw from the litigation.
The plaintiff then proceeds to trial against the non-settling defendants: Pierringer v Hoger, 124 NW 2d 106 (1963 SC Wisconsin).

The settling defendants agree to pay a sum of money, they are no longer parties to the action, and the plaintiff agrees not to pursue the non-settling defendants for more than their proportionate liability.

Since the non-settling defendants cannot be liable for more than their proportionate share of the damage, the settling defendants are not exposed to any claim for contribution from the non-settling defendants.
120 There are many variations of partial settlement agreements: CCS Corp. v Secure Energy Services Inc., 2016 ABQB 94 at para.
Pierringer agreements can be contrasted with another common type, Mary Carter agreements: Booth v Mary Carter Paint Co., 202 So 2d 8 (1967 Fl Dist CA).

In a Mary Carter agreement, the plaintiff is guaranteed a fixed recovery from the settling defendants, but the settling defendants remain parties to the action and seek to maximize recovery from the non-settling defendants.

The settling defendants' exposure is capped at the agreed amount, but the settling defendants' obligation decreases in direct proportion to any increase in the non-settling defendants' liability as determined at trial.
Justice Slatter then made this observation about Pierringer agreements (at paragraphs 125 and 127): [125]… the existing rule in Bedard v.
Amin[2010 ABCA 3], which provides that the plaintiff must account to the non-settling defendants if it “over settled”.

In other words, if a settling defendant agrees to pay the plaintiff more than the trial judge finds that settling defendant would have been liable for, the non-settling defendant is entitled to credit for that “overpayment” in order to avoid the plaintiff being double compensated. … … [127]… The effect of Bedard v.
Amin is that the risk of a Pierringer settlement falls on the plaintiff.
If the plaintiff “under-recovers” from the settling defendants, it will not be able to make up that shortfall from the non-settling defendants.
On the other hand, if the plaintiff “over-recovers” from the settling defendants (as in Bedard v.
Amin) it will not be allowed to keep the surplus.
The Court declined to overrule Bedard v.
Amin (see paragraph 148).
In Slaferek v.
TCG International Inc.
L.R.
(3d) 279 (Q.B.), Clarke J. explained a Pierringer agreement.
The plaintiffs commenced an action against the defendants who brought third parties into the action.
The plaintiff ultimately settled with the third parties (referred to by Clarke J. as “the other third parties”).

That settlement agreement contained terms which limited the liability of the other third parties in the both the main action and the contribution and indemnity proceedings (the settlement amount), and further obligated the plaintiff to indemnify the other third parties for any amount in excess of the settlement amount ultimately found owing to the plaintiff or the defendants by the other third parties.
The other third parties successfully sought from Clarke J. an order striking out the third party notice.
In the course of deciding to strike the third party notice, Clarke J. said, at pp.
285-86: Finally, the Other Third Parties describe the nature of their arrangement with the Plaintiff Darin Slaferek as a Pierringer agreement.
In that regard, they were referring to the case of Pierringer v.
2d 106 in the Supreme Court of Wisconsin.
That case involved an action arising out of an explosion wherein the settling tort feasors moved for summary judgment to dismiss cross-complaints of non-settling tort feasors for contribution.
At pp.

111-112 the Court had this to say: … The issue between the plaintiff and the non-settling defendant which should be framed by an amendment to the pleadings is the percentage of causal negligence, if any, of the non-settling defendant, but such percentage of negligence can only be determined by a proper allocation of all of the causal negligence, if any, of all the joint feasors and of the plaintiff if contributory negligence is involved.

The determination of this issue between the plaintiff and the non-settling defendant does not require the settling defendants to remain parties because the allocation, if any, of the casual negligence of the settling tort feasors is merely a part of the mechanics by which the percentage of causal negligence of the non-settling tort feasors is determined.

It makes no practical difference to the settling tort feasors what percentage of casual negligence is allocated to them because they have bought their peace in any event… Upon the trial the release should be given immediate effect as it is for contribution purposes and the judgment if any against the non-settling defendants should only be for that percentage of negligence allocated to him by the findings or the verdict.

The claim for the balance has been satisfied by the plaintiff and there is no point going through this circuitry of ordering a judgment for a larger amount and requiring the plaintiff to satisfy it… The objectives of a Pierringer agreement for the Other Third Parties of course are to set a limit upon their liability and to reduce the cost in terms of both money and personnel involved in litigating the matter.

The objective for the administration of justice is to focus the issues the Court will be required to deal with to a determination of what negligence if any can the Plaintiff Darin Slaferek bring home to Calido [the defendant] and if so what percentage of overall negligence should be borne by Calido.
The end result should be a shorter and more efficient trial.
All of these objectives in my view are ones that this Court should encourage.
Mr.
Justice Langston discussed Pierringer agreements, and Mary Carter agreements in Vandevelde v.
At p.

164, His Lordship said: The position adopted by the court in Pierringer… is consistent with the view that such agreements limit the liability of the nonsettling defendants to a question of their own several liability.
It would appear that the nonsettling defendants do not run the risk of joint liability with the settling parties, since this fact is effectively precluded by the nature of the agreement.
Langston J. then specifically commented on Slaferek v.
TCG International Inc.
L.R.
At pp.

166-67, he said: In my view Slaferek does not stand for the principle that a nonsettling defendant is precluded from third party action as against a settling defendant because of the provisions of a Pierringer agreement.
In Slaferek the plaintiff was proceeding only as against the nonsettling defendant, for its separate individual negligence.
It is clear that since the plaintiff had satisfied its claim with the settlors there was no issue of contribution.

In Slaferek the court commented on the affect of a Pierringer agreement and suggested that such agreements would focus the issues which the court will be required to deal with and those issues were the determination of what negligence if any can the plaintiff bring home to the remaining defendant, and if so, what percentage of the overall negligence should be born by the remaining defendant.

Efforts by one of several tortfeasors to settle with a plaintiff have seen the evolution of two types of agreements, one is the Pierringer agreement the other is termed a “Mary Carter” Agreement which is based on the Florida case of Booth v.
Mary Carter Paint Co.
App.).
In a Mary Carter agreement the settlor guarantees that the plaintiff will recover a sum certain and it thereby limits its own exposure.
The settlor's liability is reduced in proportion to any increase in the nonsettling defendants' liability.
The settlor remains a party to the action and may even actively help the plaintiff in its efforts to maximize the damages against the nonsettlors.

While the two types of agreements are similar in that they are settlement agreements between a plaintiff and one of several joint tortfeasors, they differ in that under a Pierringer agreement the settling defendant is no longer a party to the action and it is implicit in the agreement that the plaintiff will not pursue the nonsettling defendants for that portion, if any, of liability assessed by the trial judge against the settling party.
The settlor gains the advantage of having his liability fixed and therefore not running the risk of paying one hundred (100%) per cent of any joint and several judgment.
The issue which remains, and is central to this application is the impact which a Pierringer agreement may have on third party proceedings.
The agreement is a contract made after the commencement of litigation to which the nonsettlors are not a party but which may affect their rights adversely.

The nature of the agreement, and its timing, may effectively preclude discovery of the settlors and this would affect the nonsettlor's ability to establish negligence on the part of the settling parties.
As with a Mary Carter agreement the settling party may be actively engaged in assisting the plaintiff in its efforts to maximize the percentage of liability attributed to the nonsettling party.
A review of the decisions in Pierringer and Slaferek clearly suggest that the essence of a Pierringer agreement is the elimination of the settling parties' involvement in the litigation.
The result in both cases was the elimination of third party participation in the proceedings.

While it is clear that the defendants are not a party to the Pierringer agreements, it is equally clear that their rights may be directly affected by the obligations created in the Pierringer agreements.
The means by which third parties were eliminated in both Pierringer and Slaferek illustrates this point.
In each case the plaintiff restricted its action to the several liability of the nonsettling defendant.
In each case there were provisions for indemnifying the settling parties.
The consequence of the plaintiffs' actions was that the third parties were not exposed to any liability either from the plaintiff nor from third party actions.
Applications to strike the third party proceedings would not affect the position of the remaining parties and would clarify the issue before the courts.
Thus in a circuitous, but effective manner, the plaintiff can arbitrarily affect a nonsettling defendant's rights by completely shielding a third party's exposure.
This is clearly in keeping with the intent of Pierringer agreements and this has been the result in cases where Pierringer agreements have been utilized.
There is nothing sinister in this process since, at the end of the day, the nonsettling defendant need only address his several liability.

However the one real handicap which a nonsettling defendant faces is the issue of the manner in which he is able to prove the degree of his several negligence as it relates to the several negligence of the settling party.

Depending upon the timing of the Pierringer agreement the nonsettling defendant may be placed in the position that it is unable to discover a third party who is hastily withdrawn from the proceedings.

This issue however, is not unlike situations frequently encountered in litigation where parties may be handicapped in their ability to fully bring forth information which they view as being favourable.
The application to amend, as presently advanced by the plaintiff, purports to rely on the Pierringer agreements entered into between the plaintiff and the settling defendants.
A review of those agreements does not disclose a requirement for such an application by the plaintiff.

A review of the circumstances surrounding this application does not suggest that amending the pleadings as proposed by the plaintiff would in any way clarify the issues with which a trial court must deal.

Striking the names of the settling defendants and striking references to their potential liability is not particularly efficacious since those parties remain as litigants by virtue of their third party status.

In my view it is proper for the trial judge to have a full understanding of the complexities of the litigation, particularly in view of the fact that he may well have to deal with the apportionment of liability.
The agreements, through those portions which do require the plaintiff to make amendments, may well affect the nonsettling defendant's ability to deal with the conduct of their defence.
A partial amendment at this juncture, in my view, may well prejudice the defendants' position.
The plaintiff is clearly entitled to discontinue as against parties named in a Statement of Claim.
Such a discontinuance does not necessarily mandate that there need be an amendment to the pleadings.
Courts frequently deal with such situations and the fact that individuals identified in pleadings are no longer parties to the action does not necessarily impact upon the proceedings.

L.R.], Hart J. gave the following explanation of a Pierringer agreement: The type of settlement agreement reached by the settling parties in this case apparently originated in the case of Pierringer v.
Hoger, 124 N.W.
Wis.
S.C.

In Hudson Bay Mining & Smelting Co. v.
Fluor Daniel Wright (1997), 120 Man.
R.
Q.B.), the Manitoba Court of Queen's Bench identified the essential features of a Pierringer Agreement at page 222 to be
(a) segregation of the contracting defendant's liability
(b) satisfaction of the contracting defendant's liability to the credit of all parties to the litigation
(c) the plaintiff's ability to continue with the action against the remaining defendants

(d) the plaintiff's agreement that it will indemnify the contracting defendant for any contribution it pays to the other defendants and covenants to satisfy any judgment against the contracting defendant.
This case was followed by Rooke J. in Wright (Next Friend of) v.
VIA Rail Canada Inc.
L.R.
